text:

成化十三年秋八月當鄉試
之期應天府府尹臣崇志先
期集太學及畿甸之士二千
五百有竒于府而遣人請官

translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Yingtian Prefectural Provincial Examination

In the eighth month of autumn of the thirteenth year of the Chenghua reign (1477), at the scheduled time for the Provincial Examination, the Prefect of Yingtian Prefecture, your servant Chongzhi 崇志, gathered in advance at the prefecture more than two thousand five hundred scholars from the Directorate of Education and the metropolitan area, and dispatched a messenger to request officials to conduct the examination. His Majesty appointed the Left Mentor of the Left Secretariat of the Heir Apparent, your servant Jian 健, and the Expositor-in-waiting, your servant Jing 經. Your servants reverently received the illustrious command and traveled double-stage to get there. Upon our arrival, the Associate Examiners—Prefectural Instructors, your servants Gang 綱 and Lin 璘; County Instructors, your servants Hong 洪, Ji 冀, Wen 文, and Chu 初; and Assistant Instructors, your servants Yan 琰 and Jian 堅—along with the Surveillance Examiners, Investigating Censors, your servants Cheng 成 and Ying 英, as well as all the functionaries, had all assembled at the prefecture. Thereupon, on the seventh day of that month, we entered the examination compound together with them, and, bringing together the assembled scholars, in accordance with established…

title: 成化十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
規凡三試之而防範校閱惟
公惟慎比撤棘得中式者一
百三十五人遵
制額也故事試畢列諸執事及
中式者氏名并擇其文之尤
純者為錄進
呈既成臣健以次當序諸首竊
===
惟古者取士先德行後文藝
而後世專以文藝取之雖若
有異然其立法之初蓋亦未
甚相遠焉何則天以是理畀
之人人得之而具于心為德
行于身為行發于言論之餘
為文藝其名固異然要其實

甚相遠焉何則天以是理畀

行于身為行發于言論之餘
為文藝其名固異然要其實
punctuated:
規，凡三試之，而防範校閱，惟公惟慎。比撤棘，得中式者一百三十五人，遵制額也。故事，試畢列諸執事及中式者氏名，并擇其文之尤純者為錄進呈。既成，臣健以次當序諸首。
竊惟古者取士，先德行，後文藝，而後世專以文藝取之。雖若有異，然其立法之初，蓋亦未甚相遠焉。何則？天以是理畀之人，人得之而具于心為德，行于身為行，發于言論之餘為文藝。其名固異，然要其實，
translation_en:
… regulations, tested them in three sessions in all, and in our security precautions and the grading of papers we sought only to be impartial and circumspect. When the thorny barrier of the examination compound was removed, we had obtained one hundred and thirty-five candidates who met the standard, in compliance with the quota set by imperial decree. By precedent, when the examination is concluded, the names of all the officiating personnel and the successful candidates are listed, and the purest of their essays are selected to be compiled into a record for presentation to the throne. Now that the compilation is complete, it falls to Your Servant Jian, in order of precedence, to write a preface at its head.

I humbly reflect that in antiquity, in selecting scholars for office, moral conduct was placed first and literary art second, whereas later ages have selected them exclusively on the basis of literary art. Although this may seem different, at the original establishment of the system the two were in fact not very far apart. Why is this so? Heaven endows human beings with this Principle (li); when a person receives it and embodies it in the mind, it is virtue (de); when practiced in one's person, it is conduct (xing); and when expressed as the overflow of speech and discourse, it becomes literary art (wenyi). Their names are assuredly different, yet if we get to the heart of their reality, …

title: 成化十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
皆根本乎是理耳是故唐虞
三代盛時語德行若聖若賢
語文藝若六經之言皆卓乎
不可尚且其時選舉以鄉里
不以科目故治隆于上俗美
于下盖有由然也隋唐而下
科目取士雖專以文藝然其
===
初猶知崇尚經術根本是理
及其終也正學不明世道益
降於是始棄根本務枝葉而
艶麗竒巧之作世遂靡然趨
之殆於所謂買櫝還珠者類
焉士習如此欲其治之古若
烏可得哉欽惟我

降於是始棄根本務枝葉而
豔麗奇巧之作世遂靡然趨
之殆於所謂買櫝還珠者類
焉士習如此欲其治之古若
烏可得哉欽惟我
punctuated: 皆根本乎是理耳。是故唐、虞、三代盛時，語德行若聖若賢，語文藝若《六經》之言，皆卓乎不可尚。且其時選舉以鄉里，不以科目，故治隆于上，俗美于下，盖有由然也。隋、唐而下，科目取士雖專以文藝，然其初猶知崇尚經術，根本是理。及其終也，正學不明，世道益降，於是始棄根本、務枝葉，而艶麗竒巧之作，世遂靡然趨之，殆於所謂買櫝還珠者類焉。士習如此，欲其治之古若，烏可得哉？欽惟我
translation_en: …all are rooted in this very principle. Therefore, in the flourishing eras of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties, when speaking of moral conduct there were the sages and worthies, and when speaking of literary arts there were the words of the Six Classics—all surpassing beyond compare. Moreover, at that time selection and recommendation were carried out through the local communities rather than through examination categories; thus governance prospered above and customs were admirable below, for which there was indeed a clear reason. From the Sui and Tang dynasties onward, although the selection of scholars through examination categories relied exclusively on literary arts, in the beginning they still knew to revere classical scholarship and take this principle as the root. By the end, however, orthodox learning was obscured and the way of the world declined ever further. Thereupon people began to abandon the root and attend to the branches and leaves, and the world was swept along in pursuit of ornate and ingeniously contrived compositions—much like what is called buying the casket and returning the pearl. When the habits of scholars are such as this, even if one wished for governance to match that of antiquity, how could it be attained? I reverently reflect that our…

title: 成化十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
太祖高皇帝一天下於胡元壞亂
之餘制度之立悉法諸古雖
科目一事尚仍於近代然純
用經術不雜他道則有非近
代所能及矣
太宗文皇帝繼體守成益隆文教
嘗
===
親正五經四書性理諸書頒之
學官使天下之士非此不得
以為學而有司非此不得以
取士
列聖相承至於
今日詩書之道性理之學涵育
薰陶百有餘年俗化之美超

translation_en: …Grand Progenitor, the Exalted Emperor (Taizu, the Hongwu Emperor), unified the realm in the aftermath of the ruin and disorder of the barbarian Yuan. In establishing institutions, he modeled them all upon antiquity. Although in the single matter of the examination system he still followed recent eras, yet in purely employing classical learning without adulterating it with other ways, he achieved what recent eras could not match. The Grand Ancestor, the Cultured Emperor (Taizong, the Yongle Emperor), succeeded to the throne and maintained the dynastic achievement, further exalting civil教 (education and culture). He once personally rectified the editions of the Five Classics, the Four Books, the Compendium on Nature and Principle (Xingli), and other works, and promulgated them to the Confucian school officials, ensuring that scholars throughout the realm could not take anything other than these as their learning, and the authorities could not use anything other than these to select scholars. Through the succession of Sacred Emperors down to the present day, the Way of the Odes (Shi) and Documents (Shu) and the learning of nature and principle (xingli) have nurtured and steeped the realm for more than a hundred years; that the beauty of customs and moral transformation surpasses…

title: 成化十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
今軼古盖亦非偶然也而南
畿尤
高皇帝興王之地維新之化首先
被之士習之正文藝之純宜
有非外藩可比者臣等奉
命選士于兹於是悉以此意命
題發策既而閱之佳士果衆
===
譬之鄧林之木崑山之玉鬱
然瑩然可以柱嵓廊而禮
郊廟者比比而是因仰而嘆曰
我
皇明文教之隆億萬年無疆之休
端在是矣唐虞三代之盛且
不足言區區漢唐以下因陋

譬之鄧林之木崑山之玉鬱
然瑩然可以柱嵓廊而禮
郊廟者比比而是因仰而嘆曰
我
皇明文教之隆億萬年無疆之休
端在是矣唐虞三代之盛且
不足言區區漢唐以下因陋
punctuated: 今軼古，盖亦非偶然也。而南畿尤高皇帝興王之地，維新之化，首先被之。士習之正，文藝之純，宜有非外藩可比者。臣等奉命選士于兹，於是悉以此意命題發策。既而閱之，佳士果衆。譬之鄧林之木，崑山之玉，鬱然瑩然，可以柱嵓廊而禮郊廟者，比比而是。因仰而嘆曰：「我皇明文教之隆，億萬年無疆之休，端在是矣！唐、虞、三代之盛，且不足言；區區漢、唐以下，因陋
translation_en: … the present and outstrip antiquity—surely this is no mere coincidence. Moreover, the Southern Metropolitan Region is especially the place where the High Augustus (Emperor Taizu) rose to sovereign power, and it was the very first to receive the transformative influence of his dynastic renewal. In the rectitude of its scholars' mores and the purity of its literary arts, it naturally possesses qualities with which the outer provinces cannot compare. Having received the imperial command to select scholars here, your servants accordingly set the examination themes and posed the policy questions entirely in keeping with this intent. When we subsequently reviewed the papers, fine scholars indeed proved numerous. Compared to the timber of the Deng Forest or the jade of Mount Kun—luxuriant and lustrous—those fit to serve as pillars of the towering halls of state or as ritual vessels in the suburban sacrifices and ancestral temples are to be found everywhere. Looking up, we sighed in admiration and said: "The flourishing of our August Ming's cultural teachings, and the boundless blessings of a hundred million years, truly rest in this! Even the splendor of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties is scarcely worth mentioning; as for the paltry rule of the Han and Tang and later ages, which merely made do with crudity…

title: 成化十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
就簡之治豈能擬其萬一哉
諸士子際此
亨嘉之會登名選列固可以自
幸矣然先正有言學貴力行
不貴空言諸士子今日所事
者猶空言也繼自今宜反而
驗之是理之得于吾心者果
===
能真知歟行于吾身者果能
實踐歟發于吾口者果能彷
彿六經之言歟誠如是則德
行文藝兼而有之庶幾古人
希聖希賢之學他日由茲而
第進士擢顯官建功于時垂
名于後不惟可以無負

行文藝兼而有之庶幾古人
希聖希賢之學他日由兹而
第進士擢顯官建功于時垂

punctuated: 就簡之治，豈能擬其萬一哉！諸士子際此亨嘉之會，登名選列，固可以自幸矣。然先正有言：「學貴力行，不貴空言。」諸士子今日所事者，猶空言也。繼自今，宜反而驗之：是理之得于吾心者，果能真知歟？行于吾身者，果能實踐歟？發于吾口者，果能彷彿六經之言歟？誠如是，則德行、文藝兼而有之，庶幾古人希聖希賢之學。他日由茲而第進士、擢顯官，建功于時，垂名于後，不惟可以無負
translation_en: …make-do governance, how could it compare to even one ten-thousandth of this! Meeting with this auspicious and flourishing occasion and having their names entered onto the roster of those selected, the scholars may indeed count themselves fortunate. Yet a former worthy had a saying: "Learning prizes strenuous practice; it does not prize empty words." What the scholars have been engaged in today is still mere words. From now on, they ought to turn inward and examine themselves: as for this principle obtained in our minds, are we truly able to know it genuinely? In carrying it out in our persons, are we truly able to put it into solid practice? In uttering it from our mouths, can it truly resemble the words of the Six Classics? If it is genuinely so, then moral conduct and literary skill will both be possessed, coming close to the ancients' learning of aspiring to be sages and worthies. On a future day, proceeding from here to pass as metropolitan graduates (jinshi) and be promoted to illustrious offices, establishing merit in their own time and handing down their names to posterity, not only will they be able to avoid failing…

title: 成化十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
聖天子可以無負所志而今日主
司以言取人之失亦可以少
逭矣諸士子其勗之
左春坊左庶子劉健謹序
alt_text:
聖天子可以無負所志而今日主
司以言取人之失亦可以少
逭矣諸士子其勗之
左春坊左庶子劉〔健〕謹序
punctuated:
聖天子，可以無負所志，而今日主司以言取人之失，亦可以少逭矣。諸士子其勗之！
左春坊左庶子劉健謹序。
translation_en:
… fail the Sacred Son of Heaven and fail their own aspirations, and the fault of the present examiners in selecting men by their words may also be somewhat mitigated. May all you gentlemen exert yourselves!
Respectfully prefaced by Liu Jian 劉健, Left Mentor of the Left Secretariat of the Heir Apparent.

第壹塲

四書
古之學者為己，今之學者為人。
忠恕違道不遠，施諸己而不願，亦勿施於人。
君子深造之以道，欲其自得之也。自得之，則居之安；居之安，則資之深；資之深，則取之左右逢其原。故君子欲其自得之也。

易
夫大人者，與天地合其德，與日月合其明，與四時合其序，與鬼神合其吉凶。
天地感而萬物化生，聖人感人心而天下和平。觀其所感，而天地萬物之情可見矣。
歸奇於扐以象閏。
黃帝、堯、舜垂衣裳而天下治，盖取諸乾坤。

translation_en:
First Session

Four Books
1. "The scholars of antiquity learned for their own sake; the scholars of today learn for the sake of others." (Analects 14.24)
2. "Conscientiousness and reciprocity are not far from the Way. What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to others." (Doctrine of the Mean 13)
3. "The superior man makes his advances in learning deep by means of the Way, wishing to get hold of it in himself. Having got hold of it in himself, he abides in it calmly; abiding in it calmly, he relies on it deeply; relying on it deeply, he draws from it left and right, meeting its source everywhere. Therefore, the superior man wishes to get hold of it in himself." (Mencius 4B.14)

Book of Changes (Yi)
1. "The great man is he who is in harmony in his attributes with heaven and earth, in his brightness with the sun and moon, in his orderly procedure with the four seasons, and in his relation to good and evil fortune with the spiritual beings." (Hexagram 1, Qian, Wenyan)
2. "Heaven and earth exert their influences, and all things are transformed and brought into life. The sages influence the minds of men, and the world is brought to peace and harmony. By observing what they influence, the nature and conditions of heaven, earth, and all things can be seen." (Hexagram 31, Xian, Tuanzhuan)
3. "The remainder is placed between the fingers to represent the intercalary month." (Xici shang 9)
4. "Huangdi, Yao, and Shun simply let their upper and lower garments hang down, and the world was in order. This they probably took from the hexagrams Qian and Kun." (Xici xia 2)

translation_en:
"If he sincerely pursues the course of his virtue, the counsels offered to him will be intelligent, and his aids will be harmonious."

"The Huai and Yi rivers were regulated; Mounts Meng and Yu were brought under cultivation; the Daye marsh was confined within its bed; and the eastern plain was brought to level order."

"Until he came to possess the myriad states—how arduous this was! He sought extensively for wise men to assist his descendants. He instituted the punishments for officials to warn those in positions of authority."

"Under King Wu, these four men still went forward and enjoyed their emoluments. Afterward, together with King Wu, they grandly wielded Heaven's majesty and slew all his enemies. These four men made illustrious King Wu, who overspread the world, so that all greatly and wholly praised his virtue."

Book of Odes (Shi)

"How well the black robe befits you! When it is worn out, I will make another for you. I will go to your lodging, and when I return, I will send you a feast. How admirable is the black robe! When it is worn out, I will fashion another for you. I will go to your lodging, and when I return, I will send you a feast. How ample is the black robe! When it is worn out, I will make a new one for you. I will go to your lodging, and when I return, I will send you a feast."

"It is because he possesses it within that he resembles it without."

"The phoenixes sing on that high ridge; the parasol trees grow on that eastern slope. Lush and luxuriant is their foliage; harmonious and resonant are their notes."

"What is most powerful is to be a true man—the four quarters take him as their lesson; what is most illustrious is virtue—the hundred lords take it as their model."

translation_en:
Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu)

The armies of Qi and Song halted at Lang. Jing defeated the army of Cai at Shen, and carried off Marquis Xianwu of Cai. [Both tenth year of Duke Zhuang.]

Men of Song attacked Zheng and besieged Changge. [Fifth year of Duke Yin.] Men of Zheng came to conclude a peace. Men of Song took Changge. [Both sixth year of Duke Yin.] The Duke met the Marquis of Qi at Fang. [Ninth year of Duke Yin.] Hui led a force to join men of Qi and men of Zheng in attacking Song. The Duke defeated the army of Song at Jian. On the xinwei day, we took Gao. On the xinsi day, we took Fang. [All tenth year of Duke Yin.] Men of Qin entered Hua. The Marquis of Qi sent Guo Guifu on a mission of friendly inquiries to our court. Men of Jin and the Jiang Rong defeated Qin at Yao. Men of Jin defeated the Di at Ji. The Duke went to Qi. Men of Jin, men of Chen, and men of Zheng attacked Xu. [All thirty-third year of Duke Xi.]

The Duke met the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Chen, and the Earl of Zheng, and together made a covenant at You. [Twenty-seventh year of Duke Zhuang.] The Duke met the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Chen, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Zheng, the Baron of Xu, the Earl of Cao, and Zhao Dun of Jin; on the guiyou day, they together made a covenant at Xincheng. [Fourteenth year of Duke Wen.] Men of Jin, men of Song, men of Wei, and men of Cao together made a covenant at Qingqiu. [Twelfth year of Duke Xuan.]

The Duke met the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the Earl of Zheng, the Earl of Cao, and men of Zhu at Cheng. The Duke defeated the army of Zhu at Yan. [First year of Duke Xi.] The Marquis of Jin sent Shi Gai on a mission of friendly inquiries to our court. The Earl of Qi came to pay a court visit. The Viscount of Zhu came to pay a court visit. [All eighteenth year of Duke Cheng.]

translation_en:
Record of Rites (Liji):
"In all cases of settling the people, the land is measured to establish settlements, and the land is surveyed to settle the people; the land, the settlements, and the dwellings of the people must be in three-way proportion to one another. When there is no uncultivated land and no idle people, when food is regulated and labor is timely, the people all rest secure in their dwellings, delight in their work and encourage one another in achievement, honor their ruler and feel affection for their superiors; and only after that are schools established."
"First fix the levels and plumb-lines, and the husbandmen will not be confused."
"Therefore, that the sage is able to regard All under Heaven as one family and the Central States as one person is not a matter of mere conjecture. He must know men's feelings, open up what is righteous for them, be clear about what is advantageous to them, and comprehend what is calamitous for them; only then is he able to accomplish it."
"What the gentleman calls filial piety does not mean going to every family and seeing them daily. He brings them together at the District Archery ceremony and teaches them the rites of the District Symposium, and thus the conduct of filial piety and fraternal submission is established."

Second Session
Discourse: "Master Zeng's learning was devoted exclusively to applying the mind inwardly."

Edicts, Mandates, and Memorials [candidates are examined on one]:
An imitation of the Han edict ordering the Counselor-in-Chief, the列侯 (Marquises), the officials ranking at two thousand bushels, and the Erudites to deliberate on ways to assist the common people [first year of the Latter Era (163 BCE)].

第叁塲
策〔五道〕
問：先儒有言：「堯、舜所以為萬世法，亦率是性而已。」自古聖帝明王君臨天下，所以脩身、齊家、治國、平天下者，固不能外是性矣。其垂世立教之言，見於經傳之紀載者，可舉而言之歟？欽惟我國家列聖相承，立綱陳紀，純用是道以化成天下。

title: 成化十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
太祖高皇帝創業垂統之初即有申明五常之
誥
太宗文皇帝繼之重煕累洽文敎遂大行既
命儒臣纂集五經四書大全矣又彙萃諸儒
性理格言名曰性理大全c394至綱挈領
以嘉惠天下後世盖與前代帝王垂世
立敎之意誠異世而同符也書之首卷
備載宋儒周張邵子全書曰太極圖曰
通書曰西銘曰正蒙曰皇極經世書之
===
數子者之立言究其旨歸當與前代帝
王性理之訓我
太祖高皇帝五常之誥無以異矣亦可舉其實
而言之歟近世儒者沉酣口耳枝葉之
學以性理之論為迂闊之談至有謂聖
人之敎人性非所先者不知有天下國
家者外是性而所以脩己治人亦果别
有其道否歟諸士子佩服

translation_en: …At the very beginning of founding the dynasty and bequeathing its heritage, Grand Progenitor Emperor Gao issued his proclamation clarifying the Five Constant Virtues. Grand Ancestor Emperor Wen succeeded him; in an era of cumulative brilliance and harmony, civil teachings flourished greatly. Having already ordered Confucian courtiers to compile the Great Compendia on the Five Classics and Four Books (Wujing Sishu daquan), he also gathered together the maxims of various scholars on human nature and principle, naming the work the Great Compendium on Nature and Principle (Xingli daquan), grasping [?] the overarching principles and main threads so as to graciously benefit the empire and future generations. Indeed, his intention in handing down teachings for posterity truly matched that of the emperors and kings of former ages across different eras. The opening volumes of the work include in full the complete writings of the Song-dynasty Confucians Master Zhou [Dunyi], Master Zhang [Zai], and Master Shao [Yong]: namely, the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate (Taiji tu), Penetrating the Book of Changes (Tongshu), the Western Inscription (Ximing), Correcting Youthful Ignorance (Zhengmeng), and the Book of Supreme World-Ordering Principles (Huangji jingshi shu). When we examine the ultimate purport of the teachings established by these several masters, they should in no way differ from the instructions on nature and principle of the emperors and kings of former ages or the proclamation on the Five Constant Virtues of our Grand Progenitor Emperor Gao. Can you also cite their substance and discuss them? Scholars of recent times have been steeped in superficial learning of the mouth and ear, regarding discussions of nature and principle as impractical talk, even to the point that some claim that in the sages' teaching of men, human nature was not what came first. One wonders whether for those who possess the empire and the state, apart from this human nature, there truly is any other Way by which to cultivate oneself and govern others? You gentlemen have cherished and abided by the imperial instructions for years, and must have long studied and discussed these doctrines; set them forth in full, and do not hold back.

title: 成化十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
問易書詩春秋禮記皆載道之經自漢以
来儒者之傳註多矣何宋儒傳註一出
而前此者俱廢歟然即宋儒之傳註論
之亦有可疑者焉易傳作於程子朱子
嘗稱其義理精字數足無一毫欠闕矣
何以又有本義之作其所謂本義者果
能出程傳之外歟書傳朱子門人蔡氏
所作序稱二典禹謨朱子盖嘗是正手
澤尚新其未是正者亦有可議歟朱子
===
作詩傳自以為無復遺恨矣何以又言
易與詩中所得似雞肋焉然則其所得
者何書為多歟程子作春秋傳以微辭
隱義時措從宜者為難知故不為决然
之論胡氏傳則據孟子例以天子之事
斷之朱子謂其以義理穿鑿可指言歟
禮記一書或者以為漢儒之說其信然
歟今所取陳氏集說果能盡得記禮者
之意否歟程子嘗曰學者當以論語孟

translation_en: Question: The Book of Changes (Yi), the Book of Documents (Shu), the Book of Odes (Shi), the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu), and the Record of Rites (Liji) are all classics that convey the Way. Since the Han dynasty, commentaries and annotations by Confucian scholars have been numerous; why is it that once the commentaries and annotations of the Song Confucians appeared, all those that preceded them fell into disuse? Yet if we examine the commentaries and annotations of the Song Confucians themselves, there are also points open to doubt. The Commentary on the Changes (Yizhuan) was composed by Master Cheng [Cheng Yi 程頤], and Master Zhu [Zhu Xi 朱熹] once praised its principles as refined and its wording as sufficient, without the slightest deficiency—why then did he also compose the Original Meaning [of the周易, Benyi]? Does what he called the Original Meaning truly go beyond Cheng’s Commentary? The Commentary on the Documents (Shuzhuan) was composed by Master Zhu’s disciple Mr. Cai [Cai Chen 蔡沈]. Its preface states that Master Zhu had revised and corrected the “Two Canons” and the “Counsels of Yu,” with the traces of his hand still fresh; as for the parts he had not corrected, are there also points open to discussion? When Master Zhu composed the Commentary on the Odes (Shizhuan), he himself considered it to have left no regrets whatsoever; why then did he also say that what he had gained from the Changes and the Odes was like “chicken ribs” [of little substance but hard to discard]? If so, from which book did he gain the most? When Master Cheng composed his Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu zhuan), he regarded its subtle words, hidden meanings, and timely adaptations to circumstance as difficult to know, and therefore did not make categorical judgments. The Commentary of Mr. Hu [Hu Anguo 胡安國], however, relied on the precedent of the Mencius to judge everything as the affairs of the Son of Heaven; Master Zhu said that he forced interpretations through moral principles—can this be pointed out and explained? As for the book Record of Rites, some consider it to be the discourses of Han-dynasty Confucians; is this truly so? Can the Collected Explanations (Jishuo) of Mr. Chen [Chen Hao 陳澔], which is adopted at present, truly capture in full the intentions of those who recorded the rites, or not? Master Cheng once said: “Scholars ought to take the Analects (Lunyu) and the Mencius (Mengzi)...” …

title: 成化十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
子為本論語孟子既治則六經可不治
而明矣夫六經皆聖人妙道精義之所
在學者皓首窮之有不能造其閫奧何
以有待於論語孟子為之本歟且二書
者之所載皆孔孟言行及與其門人問
荅之辭又何以與六經之言相入歟諸
士子窮經有年會其異而歸諸同以待
主司之問正今日事也其悉心以對
問人君所以致天下之治無他術在天下
===
之吏各稱其任而已然位公卿者不能
皆咎夔列庶職者不能皆宅俊親昵者
顯則疏遠者隱矣便佞者進則方正者
退矣其流至於官冗政貪吏怨民弊而
不可止此考課之法所由立也稽之於
古三載考績三考黜陟幽明唐虞之制
也何鯀九載弗成而始罪禹九州攸同
而始賞不其簡歟三歲計吏治九年大
明黜陟成周之制也何又曰月歲終之

問：人君所以致天下之治，無他術，在天下之吏各稱其任而已。然位公卿者不能皆咎、夔，列庶職者不能皆宅俊。親昵者顯，則疏遠者隱矣；便佞者進，則方正者退矣。其流至於官冗政貪，吏怨民弊，而不可止，此考課之法所由立也。稽之於古，「三載考績，三考黜陟幽明」，唐、虞之制也。何鯀九載弗成而始罪，禹九州攸同而始賞，不其簡歟？「三歲計吏治，九年大明黜陟」，成周之制也。何又曰月、歲終之
translation_en:
… [Master Cheng once said that scholars should take the Analects and the] Mencius (Mengzi) as the foundation; once the Analects and the Mencius are mastered, then the Six Classics can be understood without separate study." Now, the Six Classics are all wherein the subtle Way and refined principles of the sages reside; even scholars who exhaust their lives until their hair turns white studying them are sometimes unable to reach their innermost depths. Why then must one rely upon taking the Analects and the Mencius as their foundation? Moreover, what is recorded in these two books consists entirely of the words and deeds of Confucius and Mencius, along with their questions and answers with their disciples; how is it that they mutually penetrate the words of the Six Classics? You gentlemen have thoroughly studied the Classics for years, bringing together their differences and reducing them to a common unity in anticipation of the examiners' questions—this is precisely the business of today. Respond with all your heart.

Question: The means by which a ruler brings about order in the realm requires no other art than that the officials of the realm each match their responsibilities, and nothing more. Yet those who occupy the positions of Dukes and Ministers cannot all be like Gao Yao and Kui, and those arrayed in the various offices cannot all be settled men of eminence. When the intimate and favored become prominent, the distant and estranged go into hiding; when the glib and flattering advance, the upright and square-dealing retreat. The degeneration of this reaches the point where offices are superfluous and governance is rapacious, officials are resentful and the people are exhausted, and it cannot be stopped. This is why the system of merit evaluation (kaoke) was established. Examining into antiquity, "every three years to examine achievements, and after three examinations to demote the unenlightened and promote the enlightened" was the institution of Tang and Yu [Yao and Shun]. Why was it that Gun was only punished after nine years without success, and Yu was only rewarded after the Nine Provinces were brought into harmony—was that not overly simple? "Every three years to reckon the governance of officials, and after nine years to make a great clarification of demotions and promotions" was the institution of flourishing Zhou. Why then was there also mention of the rectifications at the end of the month and the end of the year…

title: 成化十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
有正六計八職之旁稽不其煩歟然後
世稱人才之盛致治之美必曰唐虞成
周豈聖王之御世固自有其要而不在
於煩簡歟周之後有漢說者謂其考課
猶有古意何以見之其得人致治可指
議歟漢之後有唐有宋殿最益密其視
古固有間然亦嘗得人致治歟至若臣
下建明京房專欲任法崔林專欲任人
劉邵七十二條杜預六優六劣其說然
===
歟否歟亦可行之於今歟方今考課既
有三載九年之考又有
朝覲會同之法盖優劣本於長吏而當否察
於憲臺覈實總於吏部而予奪制在
朝廷盖即唐虞成周之遺意也然是非或出
於妬口好惡或匪其公心微瑕或至於
被斥而巨蠹或得以幸存所以又廑
九重今日之慮也伊欲使吏職克稱士風以
淳治效如唐虞成周之盛如之何則可

punctuated: 有正，六計八職之旁稽，不其煩歟？然後世稱人才之盛、致治之美，必曰唐虞、成周，豈聖王之御世，固自有其要，而不在於煩簡歟？周之後有漢，說者謂其考課猶有古意，何以見之？其得人致治可指議歟？漢之後有唐、有宋，殿最益密，其視古固有間，然亦嘗得人致治歟？至若臣下建明，京房專欲任法，崔林專欲任人，劉邵七十二條，杜預六優六劣，其說然歟否歟？亦可行之於今歟？方今考課，既有三載、九年之考，又有朝覲會同之法。盖優劣本於長吏，而當否察於憲臺，覈實總於吏部，而予奪制在朝廷，盖即唐虞、成周之遺意也。然是非或出於妬口，好惡或匪其公心，微瑕或至於被斥，而巨蠹或得以幸存，所以又廑九重今日之慮也。伊欲使吏職克稱，士風以淳，治效如唐虞、成周之盛，如之何則可？
translation_en: …rectifications, and the collateral inspections of the six criteria of evaluation (liuji) and the eight administrative functions (bazhi)—was that not overly complex? Yet when later ages praise the flourishing of men of talent and the excellence of governance achieved, they invariably speak of Tang, Yu, and the accomplished Zhou. Could it be that in ruling the world, the sage kings inherently possessed their own essentials, which did not lie in complexity or simplicity? After the Zhou came the Han. Commentators say that its evaluation of officials (kaoke) still retained the spirit of antiquity; how can this be seen? Can its obtaining of capable men and achieving of good governance be pointed out and discussed? After the Han came the Tang and the Song, whose rankings of demerit and merit (dianzui) grew ever more detailed. Compared to antiquity there was certainly a gap, yet did they also at times obtain capable men and achieve good governance? As for the proposals set forth by officials: Jing Fang 京房 wished to rely exclusively on fixed methods; Cui Lin 崔林 wished to rely exclusively on men; Liu Shao 劉邵 proposed seventy-two articles; and Du Yu 杜預 proposed counting six merits and six demerits. Were their theories right or wrong? And can they also be practiced today? At present, in the evaluation of officials, there are already the evaluations at three years and nine years, and there is also the regulation for joint assessment at court audiences (chaojin huitong). For the rating of superiority and inferiority originates with the senior local officials, its appropriateness is investigated by the Censorate (Xiantai), verification of the facts is summarized by the Ministry of Personnel (Libu), and the power to grant or deprive rests with the Royal Court—which is indeed the inherited intent of Tang, Yu, and the accomplished Zhou. Yet judgments of right and wrong sometimes issue from envious mouths, likes and dislikes sometimes do not come from an impartial mind, those with minor flaws sometimes end up being dismissed, while great parasites sometimes manage by luck to survive. This is why it again engages the concern of the Ninefold Palace (the Emperor) today. If we wish to cause administrative duties to be fully matched by competence, the ethos of the literati to become pure, and the results of governance to equal the flourishing of Tang, Yu, and the accomplished Zhou, how may this be achieved?

title: 成化十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
諸士子強學待問議之必熟矣願紬繹
以對
問
朝廷設科求賢固欲得真才以資化理也然
真才之成必由學問之正所謂正學者
聖賢之學是已其工夫次第可得而詳
言歟今之學者大率有二博記誦工文
辭由是二者而不已焉聖賢之學果不
外是而可以得真才歟古之真才見用
===
於世者在唐虞三代若皐陶伊傅周召
諸君子今即其言行之存尚可考見其
學問之正歟自是而下曰漢曰唐曰宋
才不古若矣而隨世以就功名之士若
漢之蕭曹丙魏唐之房杜姚宋宋之韓
范富歐者亦可因其人而槩言其學問
之非正歟孔孟既沒正學寥寥至宋而
始續其最著者周程張朱數子學問之
正無愧古人而不得見用於世然使之

辭由是二者而不已焉聖賢之學果不
外是而可以得真才歟古之真才見用
===
於世者在唐虞三代若臯陶伊傅周召
諸君子今即其言行之存尚可考見其
學問之正歟自是而下曰漢曰唐曰宋
才不古若矣而隨世以就功名之士若
漢之蕭曹丙魏唐之房杜姚宋宋之韓
范富歐者亦可因其人而槩言其學問
之非正歟孔孟既沒正學寥寥至宋而
始續其最著者周程張朱數子學問之
正無愧古人而不得見用於世然使之
punctuated:
諸士子強學待問，議之必熟矣，願紬繹以對。

問：朝廷設科求賢，固欲得真才以資化理也。然真才之成，必由學問之正。所謂正學者，聖賢之學是已，其工夫次第可得而詳言歟？今之學者大率有二：博記誦，工文辭。由是二者而不已焉，聖賢之學果不外是而可以得真才歟？古之真才見用於世者，在唐、虞、三代，若皐陶、伊、傅、周、召諸君子，今即其言行之存，尚可考見其學問之正歟？自是而下，曰漢、曰唐、曰宋，才不古若矣。而隨世以就功名之士，若漢之蕭、曹、丙、魏，唐之房、杜、姚、宋，宋之韓、范、富、歐者，亦可因其人而槩言其學問之非正歟？孔、孟既沒，正學寥寥，至宋而始續。其最著者，周、程、張、朱數子，學問之正，無愧古人，而不得見用於世。然使之
translation_en:
You scholars have studied diligently in anticipation of being questioned and must have deliberated thoroughly upon these matters; we hope you will draw out your thoughts and reply in full.

Question: When the imperial court establishes examination categories to seek the worthy, it certainly wishes to obtain true talent to assist in transformative governance. Yet the formation of true talent must come from orthodoxy in learning and inquiry. What is called orthodox learning is simply the learning of the sages and worthies; can its practical efforts and sequential stages be spoken of in detail? Scholars of today generally fall into two types: those who broaden their memorization and recitation, and those who hone their literary compositions. If one pursues these two without ceasing, does the learning of the sages and worthies indeed lie nowhere outside of this, and can true talent be obtained thereby? As for the true talents of antiquity who were employed in the world—such as the noble men Gao Yao 皐陶, Yi Yin 伊尹, Fu Yue 傅說, the Duke of Zhou 周公, and the Duke of Shao 召公 in the eras of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties—can we today, by examining their surviving words and deeds, still investigate and see the orthodoxy of their learning? From that time downward, in the Han, the Tang, and the Song, talent no longer matched antiquity. Yet regarding those scholars who adapted to their times to achieve merit and fame—such as Xiao He 蕭何, Cao Shen 曹參, Bing Ji 丙吉, and Wei Xiang 魏相 of the Han; Fang Xuanling 房玄齡, Du Ruhui 杜如晦, Yao Chong 姚崇, and Song Jing 宋璟 of the Tang; and Han Qi 韓琦, Fan Zhongyan 范仲淹, Fu Bi 富弼, and Ouyang Xiu 歐陽修 of the Song—can one also, on account of the men themselves, make a sweeping judgment that their learning was not orthodox? After Confucius 孔子 and Mencius 孟子 passed away, orthodox learning fell silent and sparse until the Song, when it was first resumed. Of its most prominent figures—the several masters Zhou Dunyi 周敦頤, the Cheng brothers 程顥/程頤, Zhang Zai 張載, and Zhu Xi 朱熹—the orthodoxy of their learning leaves them with nothing to be ashamed of before the ancients, yet they were not employed in the world. Still, had they been…

title: 成化十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
得用其措諸事業果能追配唐虞三代
之諸君子歟近世儒者有言傳記中人
才傑然可觀以道理觀之只是偏才聖
人則圓融渾全百理皆具夫人之才一
也何以有二者之分歟且圓融渾全百
理皆具盖即所謂真才也人能由聖賢
之學亦可馴致之歟諸士子生長畿甸
涵育
聖化最先且久不知今日之所以學問者果聖
===

願明以告我茲將考其真才以仰副
聖天子設科求賢之盛意焉
問漢之賢君莫賢於文帝而賈誼當其盛
時上策治安乃至流涕太息誼豈固為
是矯激之語哉亦獻忠報國之心耳欽
惟
皇上至仁大德遠同堯舜文帝盖不足以擬之
矣而求言願治之心方拳拳焉天下之

得用，其措諸事業，果能追配唐、虞、三代之諸君子歟？近世儒者有言：「傳記中人才傑然可觀，以道理觀之，只是偏才；聖人則圓融渾全，百理皆具。」夫人之才一也，何以有二者之分歟？且圓融渾全、百理皆具，盖即所謂真才也，人能由聖賢之學，亦可馴致之歟？諸士子生長畿甸，涵育聖化，最先且久，不知今日之所以學問者，果聖賢之學歟？抑猶未免記誦文辭之習也？願明以告我，茲將考其真才，以仰副聖天子設科求賢之盛意焉。

問：漢之賢君莫賢於文帝，而賈誼當其盛時，上策治安，乃至流涕太息。誼豈固為是矯激之語哉？亦獻忠報國之心耳。欽惟皇上至仁大德，遠同堯、舜，文帝盖不足以擬之矣，而求言願治之心方拳拳焉，天下之
translation_en:
… been employed, could the achievements they put into practice truly have rivaled those of the noble men of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties? A Confucian scholar of recent times remarked: "The men of talent in historical biographies are outstanding and impressive to behold, yet viewed in the light of moral principle, they are merely partial talents; the sages, by contrast, are harmoniously complete and perfectly whole, endowed with all principles." Now, human talent is one and the same; why is there this division between the two? Moreover, being harmoniously complete, perfectly whole, and endowed with all principles is surely what we call true talent—if a person follows the learning of the sages and worthies, can he gradually attain this as well? You gentlemen were born and raised in the metropolitan region, and have been nourished by the Sage's transforming influence earliest and longest. I do not know whether what you pursue in your learning today is truly the learning of the sages and worthies, or whether it still does not escape the habit of rote memorization and literary composition. Please explain this to me clearly; from this I shall examine your true talent, so as to respectfully fulfill the Sacred Son of Heaven's grand intention in establishing the examinations to seek out the worthy.

Question: Among the worthy rulers of the Han, none was worthier than Emperor Wen (Wendi 文帝), yet during his flourishing reign Jia Yi 賈誼 submitted a policy memorial on peace and order in which he went so far as to weep and sigh deeply. Did Yi deliberately make such extreme and provocative statements? It was simply out of a heart devoted to offering loyalty and repaying the state. Reverently considering His Majesty, whose supreme benevolence and great virtue match those of Yao 堯 and Shun 舜 in distant antiquity—such that Emperor Wen is hardly worthy of comparison—his heart is nonetheless earnestly devoted to seeking counsel and desiring good governance. title: 成化十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
士孰不願獻其芹曝之愚哉故即今日
有司之務試與諸士子商之夫理國在
人才掄才在銓選今之銓選非無法也
然拘資格則賢愚以混進事保薦則名
實或未符足國在財賦理財在會計今
之會計非無制也然征輸之力亦已竭
而調發之用恒不足邊防威虜選將練
兵其術也今將多出於膏粱而兵多歸
於私役刑罰輔治專人明法其道也今
===
政或分於多門而罪或失於不中學校
本以明教化而異端之徒尚噓誣世之
燄鄉飲本以興禮讓而姦宄之輩猶扇
訐上之風以至士風之弊廉耻不顧有
乞墦拜塵者矣民俗之弊奢侈無節有
帝服后飾者矣凡若此者未易徧舉皆
今之執政者所欲願聞也變通張弛不
失
今日之法舉行禁厲有合古人之意殆必有

punctuated: 士，孰不願獻其芹曝之愚哉？故即今日有司之務，試與諸士子商之。夫理國在人才，掄才在銓選，今之銓選非無法也；然拘資格則賢愚以混進，事保薦則名實或未符。足國在財賦，理財在會計，今之會計非無制也；然征輸之力亦已竭，而調發之用恒不足。邊防威虜，選將練兵其術也；今將多出於膏粱，而兵多歸於私役。刑罰輔治，專人明法其道也；今政或分於多門，而罪或失於不中。學校本以明教化，而異端之徒尚噓誣世之燄；鄉飲本以興禮讓，而姦宄之輩猶扇訐上之風。以至士風之弊，廉耻不顧，有乞墦拜塵者矣；民俗之弊，奢侈無節，有帝服后飾者矣。凡若此者，未易徧舉，皆今之執政者所欲願聞也。變通張弛，不失今日之法；舉行禁厲，有合古人之意，殆必有
translation_en:
… scholars of the realm would not wish to offer up their humble, earnest counsel, like a gift of wild celery or basking in the sun? Therefore, taking up the current duties of the authorities, let us discuss them with you scholars.

Now, ordering the state lies in human talent, and selecting talent lies in personnel evaluation and appointment. Present-day personnel selection is not without regulations; yet if one is bound by seniority and qualifications, the worthy and the foolish advance together indiscriminatingly, whereas if one relies on guaranteed recommendations, reputation and reality sometimes fail to correspond. Enriching the state lies in fiscal revenues, and managing finances lies in accounting. Present-day accounting is not without institutions; yet the people's capacity to pay taxes and render transport service is already exhausted, while the funds needed for requisitions and disbursements are constantly insufficient. In frontier defense and overawing the northern caitiffs, the art lies in selecting generals and training troops; yet today generals mostly come from wealthy, pampered families, and soldiers are mostly diverted into private labor service. In using punishments and penalties to assist governance, the way lies in assigning dedicated officials and clarifying the laws; yet today administration is sometimes divided among multiple agencies, and sentencing sometimes errs by failing to hit the mark of justice. Schools were originally established to clarify moral transformation through education, yet followers of heterodox teachings still fan the flames that deceive the world; the Community Libation Ceremony (xiangyin) was originally instituted to promote ritual deference, yet wicked and treacherous sorts still stir up the trend of denouncing their superiors. This extends even to the abuses in literati ethos, where integrity and shame are disregarded, and there are those who beg among tombs and bow to the dust of powerful carriages; and to the abuses in popular customs, where extravagance knows no restraint, and there are those who wear imperial robes and empresses' ornaments.

Matters such as all these cannot easily be enumerated in full, yet they are all things that those who hold the reins of government today eagerly wish to hear about. To adapt and alternate between stringency and leniency without losing sight of the laws of the present day; and to put measures into practice and enforce prohibitions so as to accord with the intentions of the ancients—there must surely be…

text:
第壹場
四書義
古之學者為已今之學者為人
潘密
同考試官教諭馬批此題似易而難學者率
不究心故場中逞辭而無倫者比比求其理致純粹文辭
明整者僅見此篇宜錄之以為學者式
同考試官教諭季批此題場中作者多泛泛

古今之人為學雖同而用心則異夫人必有學
古今一致固無不同也然或以之為已或以之
為人其用心之得失豈不有異哉今夫天賦人
以性均善而無惡但人於形生神發之後欲動
情勝而失之者衆非學則無以復其初也是故
古之人知其然以吾性之未復也格物致知而

考試官左庶子劉批：分析為已為人，語精而意到。

古今之人為學雖同，而用心則異。夫人必有學，古今一致，固無不同也。然或以之為已，或以之為人，其用心之得失，豈不有異哉？今夫天賦人以性，均善而無惡。但人於形生神發之後，欲動情勝，而失之者衆，非學則無以復其初也。是故古之人知其然，以吾性之未復也，格物致知，而
translation_en:
First Session
Expositions on the Four Books
"In ancient times men learned for themselves; nowadays men learn for the approbation of others." (Analects 14.24)
Pan Mi 潘密

Comment by Associate Examiner, Instructor (jiaoyu) Ma 馬: This topic seems easy yet is difficult, and scholars generally do not investigate its core meaning deeply. Thus in the examination hall, those who show off their rhetoric without coherence are everywhere. Although men of ancient and modern times are the same in pursuing learning, the intentions they apply to it are different. That a person must engage in learning is consistent across antiquity and the present, and certainly does not differ. Yet some pursue it for themselves, while others pursue it for the approbation of others—how could the merits and defects of their intentions not be different? text:
察之於事物之間誠意正心而驗之於躬行之
際理有未合孳孳焉益精其慮必使性之體與
吾心相涵也事有未當勉勉焉益致其力必使
性之用與吾身相安也古之人學欲得之於已
如此非為已而何今之人則不然以吾名之未
立也學雖事於致知不急乎性情之得功雖用
於力行徒以為利祿之資善有未著蚤夜而思
之務表白于人焉行有未聞旦暮而慮之務昭
彰于外焉今人之學欲見知於人如此非為人

性情之間但其用心有為已為人之別耳聖人
對舉而警戒之猶如此其至乃若後世學者務
為入耳出口之學有不識性情為何物者宜何
如其警戒哉

察之於事物之間，誠意正心而驗之於躬行之際。理有未合，孳孳焉益精其慮，必使性之體與吾心相涵也；事有未當，勉勉焉益致其力，必使性之用與吾身相安也。古之人學欲得之於已如此，非為已而何？今之人則不然。以吾名之未立也，學雖事於致知，不急乎性情之得；功雖用於力行，徒以為利祿之資。善有未著，蚤夜而思之，務表白于人焉；行有未聞，旦暮而慮之，務昭彰于外焉。今人之學欲見知於人如此，非為人而何？吁！學一也，為已為人之間，而得失之迹于焉以分。立心之始，學者可不致其謹歟？抑又論之，春秋之時，去古未遠，學者猶知致力于心身性情之間，但其用心有為已為人之別耳。聖人對舉而警戒之，猶如此其至；乃若後世學者，務為入耳出口之學，有不識性情為何物者，宜何如其警戒哉？

「忠恕違道不遠，施諸已而不願，亦勿施於人。」
translation_en:
…examine it amidst affairs and things; they make their intentions sincere and rectify their minds, verifying it in the course of personal practice. When principle is not yet fully met, they tirelessly refine their thoughts all the more, determined that the substance of human nature be mutually steeped with their own minds; when affairs are not yet properly handled, they assiduously exert their strength all the more, determined that the function of human nature be at ease with their own persons. The ancients pursued learning with the desire to attain it within themselves like this—what was this if not learning for oneself? People of today, however, are not so. Thinking that their reputation is not yet established, although their learning engages in the extension of knowledge, they are not urgent about attaining their nature and feelings; although their effort is applied to strenuous practice, they merely treat it as a means to gain profit and emolument. When their goodness is not yet manifest, they ponder it morning and night, striving to display it before others; when their conduct is not yet renowned, they worry over it from dawn to dusk, striving to make it conspicuous to the outside world. People of today pursue learning with the desire to be known by others like this—what is this if not learning for the sake of others? Alas! Learning is one, yet between doing it for oneself and doing it for others, the traces of success and failure divide right here. At the very beginning of establishing one's mind, how can learners not exercise their utmost caution? Furthermore, if we discuss this further: in the Spring and Autumn period, which was not yet far removed from antiquity, learners still knew to devote their strength to matters of mind, body, nature, and feelings, and the difference lay only in whether their intention was for themselves or for others. Even so, the Sage contrasted the two and admonished them to such an extreme degree; as for learners of later ages, who occupy themselves with learning that merely enters the ear and exits the mouth, and among whom there are some who do not even know what nature and feelings are—how much more severe should the admonition for them be!

"Conscientiousness and reciprocity are not far from the Way. What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to others."

Extending its discussion of the principle that "in practicing the Way, one does not distance oneself from human beings," the Doctrine of the Mean states that the Way is nothing other than the principle of what ought to be. text:
以忠恕推之夫婦長幼朋友之際有以得其當
然之則而施無不宜則去是道也為近矣忠恕
之違道不遠如此而其事果何如哉是故如人
以無禮之事施諸已已所不願也則必以此度
人之心亦勿以此無禮施之焉人以不忠之事
加諸我我所不欲也則必以此度人之心亦勿
以此不忠加之焉吁盡已之心而推以及人如
此雖未可遽謂之道然亦道之勉然者耳自是
而往其相違也夫何遠哉抑聖賢於忠恕言之

則居之安居之安則資之深資之深則取
之左右逢其原故君子欲其自得之也

punctuated:
以忠恕推之夫婦、長幼、朋友之際，有以得其當然之則，而施無不宜，則去是道也為近矣。忠恕之違道不遠如此，而其事果何如哉？是故，如人以無禮之事施諸已，已所不願也，則必以此度人之心，亦勿以此無禮施之焉；人以不忠之事加諸我，我所不欲也，則必以此度人之心，亦勿以此不忠加之焉。吁！盡已之心而推以及人如此，雖未可遽謂之道，然亦道之勉然者耳。自是而往，其相違也，夫何遠哉？抑聖賢於忠恕，言之不一：有以學者事言者，有以聖人事言者。《中庸》之言，下學工夫，盖學者事也，故曰：「違道不遠。」《論語》之言，即誠即仁，盖聖人事也，故曰：「夫子之道，忠恕而已矣。」其分固截然不同，然學者誠能由下學之忠恕而勉之，工夫既至，涵養既深，何聖人之忠恕不可及乎？

「君子深造之以道，欲其自得之也。自得之，則居之安；居之安，則資之深；資之深，則取之左右逢其原。故君子欲其自得之也。」
translation_en:
…extend them with conscientiousness and reciprocity to the relations between husband and wife, elder and younger, and friend and friend, so as to attain their proper norms and act with unfailing appropriateness, then one's distance from this Way will be slight indeed. Since conscientiousness and reciprocity are thus not far from the Way, what then does their practice actually entail? Therefore, if others inflict discourtesy upon oneself, which one does not wish for oneself, one must measure the hearts of others by this and likewise refrain from inflicting such discourtesy upon them; if others impose disloyalty upon me, which I do not desire for myself, I must measure the hearts of others by this and likewise refrain from imposing such disloyalty upon them. Ah! Exhausting one's own heart and extending it to others in this manner—though it cannot immediately be called the Way itself, it is nonetheless the diligent practice of the Way. Proceeding from this, how could the distance between them be far at all? Moreover, the sages and worthies have spoken of conscientiousness and reciprocity in more than one manner: sometimes speaking of them as the business of the learner, and sometimes as the business of the sage. What is said in the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong) concerns the effort of lower-level learning, which is the business of the learner; hence it says, "they are not far from the Way." What is said in the Analects (Lunyu) is identical with sincerity and humanity, which is the business of the sage; hence it says, "The Way of our Master is none other than conscientiousness and reciprocity." Their levels are indeed distinctly different; yet if the learner can truly exert himself starting from the conscientiousness and reciprocity of lower-level learning, once his effort reaches its culmination and his self-cultivation becomes deep, why should the conscientiousness and reciprocity of the sage be beyond his reach?

"The superior man makes his advances in learning deeply according to the right way, wishing to get hold of it as in himself. Having got hold of it in himself, he abides in it calmly; abiding in it calmly, he relies on it deeply; relying on it deeply, he draws from it on the left and right, meeting its source everywhere. Therefore, the superior man wishes to get hold of it as in himself."

In discussing how the gentleman exerts himself in learning through the proper method because he wishes to acquire it in himself, one must set forth its effects in sequence and trace back his original intent. Now, learning certainly values acquiring truth within oneself; yet without reaching deeply by following the method of progressive advancement, how could one bring about the effect of acquiring it in oneself? Rightly did Mencius (Mengzi 孟子) speak of this from beginning to end in order to instruct others. Now, in a person's pursuit of the Way, nothing comes before learning, and learning must follow a method if it is to be good learning. translation_en:
…comprehend it in the mind. Because the learning of the noble man is like this, whereas formerly he was benighted and gained nothing, now his mind and principle fuse together and there is nothing he does not attain; consequently, that whereby he abides in it is secure, firm, and unshakeable. Whereas formerly he was unsettled and ill at ease, now external things and his nature unite and there is nowhere he is not at ease; consequently, that upon which he relies is profound, far-reaching, and inexhaustible. Once that upon which he relies is profound, in daily usage, when he draws upon it to the left, on the left he never fails to encounter the root of what sustains him; when he draws upon it to the right, on the right he never fails to meet the source of what he relies upon. Now, when learning reaches the point of personal realization, its effects manifest in due order without waiting for artificial arrangement or contrivance—such being the case, is this not why the learning of the noble man necessarily seeks to attain it for oneself! In general, principle cannot be sought through shallow haste, and learning cannot be advanced through arbitrary whim. To reach deeply into it and necessarily do so by the proper Way—this is Mencius's utmost intention in teaching people. If the student engages in this and attains something therein, then a single thread will run through the purport of the Seven Books: all the sayings on the goodness of human nature and nourishing the vital breath, as well as the discussions on knowing Heaven and serving Heaven, will be silently comprehended beyond words. When former Confucian scholars spoke of "the knowledge of moral nature not sprouting from hearing and seeing," did they not mean this?

text:
同考試官教諭馬批此篇能體貼本義成文見
理精切措辭雅健非深於易者弗能是宜録出
同考試官教諭李批此題本平易學者多忽略
故佳作絕少惟此篇講貫詳明措詞允當特表而出之
考試官侍讀周批說大人德合造化詞理精到
非有見者不能
考試官左庶子劉批大人能與造化合以其無私
耳此作得之
大人之心純乎道故與造化之理無不合夫人
===
與造化之理不相合者以人有私焉耳大人之
心無私而純乎道豈不與之相合而無間哉文
言聖人釋乾九五之大人謂夫人與天地日月
四時鬼神本無二理特蔽於有我之私是以梏
於形體而不能相通大人之心至公無私以道
為體曽何彼此之可言哉是故天覆于上地載
于下天地之德覆載無私也大人則高明配天
博厚配地與之合其德焉日生于東月生于西
日月之明照臨無私也大人則智周萬物光被

Its grasp of principle is precise and incisive, and its diction is elegant and vigorous. None but one deeply versed in the *Changes* (*Yi*) could have written it; it ought to be selected for recording.
Associate Examiner and Instructor Li李 comments: This topic is inherently straightforward, so scholars mostly overlook it, and consequently fine compositions on it are exceedingly rare. Only this essay explicates the theme thoroughly and clearly, with apt and fitting phrasing; I specially single it out for distinction.
Examiner and Reader-in-Waiting Zhou周 comments: In explaining how the virtue of the Great Man accords with the creative transformations of nature, both the phrasing and the reasoning reach the utmost precision—something impossible without true insight.
Examiner and Left Mentor Liu劉 comments: That the Great Man is able to accord with the creative transformations of nature is simply because he has no selfishness; this composition has grasped that point.
Because the mind of the Great Man is purely devoted to the Way, there is nothing in which it fails to accord with the principle of the creative transformations of nature. Now, the reason why ordinary people do not accord with the principle of the creative transformations is simply that they harbor selfishness. Since the mind of the Great Man is free from selfishness and purely devoted to the Way, how could it not accord with them without the slightest gap? In the "Words of the Text" ("Wenyan"), when the Sage explains the "Great Man" of the Nine in the Fifth place of the *Qian* hexagram, he means that human beings and Heaven and Earth, the sun and moon, the four seasons, and the ghosts and spirits originally do not have two different principles; it is only because people are obscured by the selfishness of ego that they are fettered by their physical forms and cannot communicate with them. The mind of the Great Man is utterly impartial and selfless, taking the Way as its substance—how could one even speak of any division between "this" and "that"? Therefore, Heaven covers from above and Earth supports from below; the virtue of Heaven and Earth is to cover and support without selfishness. The Great Man, in his lofty brilliance, matches Heaven, and in his broad thickness, matches Earth, thereby according with their virtue. The sun rises in the east and the moon rises in the west; the brightness of the sun and moon shines down without selfishness. 四表與之合其明焉至若春夏秋冬流行于四
時陽舒陰慘未嘗失其序而大人則仁育義正
之公一四時舒慘之公也序其有不合乎陰屈
陽伸運用於鬼神福善禍淫未嘗乖其理而大
人則賞善罰惡之公一鬼神禍福之公也吉凶
其有不合乎吁大人至公無私之心與天地日
月四時鬼神無往而不合如此此所以尊居九
五而為天下之所利見也歟抑又論之聖人傳

易者宜合而觀之

四表，與之合其明焉。至若春夏秋冬，流行于四時，陽舒陰慘，未嘗失其序；而大人則仁育義正之公，一四時舒慘之公也，序其有不合乎？陰屈陽伸，運用於鬼神，福善禍淫，未嘗乖其理；而大人則賞善罰惡之公，一鬼神禍福之公也，吉凶其有不合乎？吁！大人至公無私之心，與天地、日月、四時、鬼神無往而不合如此，此所以尊居九五，而為天下之所利見也歟！抑又論之，聖人傳《乾》《文言》於九五，聖人屢有以賛之：既擬以雲龍風虎之盛，復稱以位乎天德之尊，至此又言其與天地、日月、四時、鬼神有合焉，其賛之也至矣。他日稱堯，亦嘗曰：「大哉，堯之為君也！巍巍乎！惟天為大，惟堯則之。」盖天者，理之盡而誠之至者也。賛聖人而擬之天，名言之妙，豈復有加哉？學《易》者宜合而觀之。

translation_en:
… the four quarters, and thus unites with their brilliance. As for spring, summer, autumn, and winter, as they circulate through the four seasons, the expansion of yang and the severity of yin never lose their proper order; and the great man's impartiality in nurturing through benevolence and rectifying through righteousness is one and the same as the four seasons' impartiality in expansion and severity—how could his order fail to unite with theirs? The contraction of yin and the extension of yang operate through ghosts and spirits, blessing the good and bringing calamity to the licentious without ever violating their principle; and the great man's impartiality in rewarding the good and punishing the evil is one and the same as the ghosts and spirits' impartiality in bestowing fortune and misfortune—how could his auspices and omens fail to unite with theirs? Ah! Because the great man's supremely impartial and selfless mind unites everywhere in this manner with Heaven and Earth, the sun and moon, the four seasons, and ghosts and spirits, is this not why he occupies the exalted position of the Nine in the Fifth Place, and why it is advantageous for all under Heaven to see him? Furthermore, let us consider this: when the Sage wrote the commentary of the Words of the Text (Wenyan) on the hexagram Qian for the Nine in the Fifth Place, he repeatedly praised the Sage-ruler: having first compared him to the flourishing of clouds following the dragon and wind following the tiger, and then extolled him as occupying the exalted position of heavenly virtue, here he goes on to say that he unites with Heaven and Earth, the sun and moon, the four seasons, and ghosts and spirits—his praise of him is ultimate indeed! On another occasion, when praising Yao, he also said: "Great indeed was Yao as a sovereign! How lofty! Only Heaven is great, and only Yao modeled himself upon it." For Heaven is the exhaustion of principle and the utmost of sincerity. In praising the Sage and comparing him to Heaven, how could anything further be added to the subtlety of such famous words? Those who study the Book of Changes (Yi) ought to examine these passages together.

"The Yellow Emperor (Huangdi), Yao, and Shun let their upper and lower garments hang down and all under Heaven was governed; this they probably took from the hexagrams Qian and Kun."

Only this essay brings out the purport of how the sages adapted to change while practicing non-action. It deeply accords with the meaning of the topic and is especially worthy of being selected for publication.
Comment by Examiner Academician Reader-in-waiting Zhou: The sages changed what the people could not change for themselves, and therefore all under Heaven became orderly of its own accord—this essay has expressed it completely.

The governance of the sages through adapting to change and non-action was presumably drawn from the emblems of transformation and non-action. Now Qian and Kun are things that transform and yet act without deliberate effort; when the Yellow Emperor (Huangdi), Yao, and Shun adapted to the changes in the customs of the people and brought about governance through non-action, did they not draw this from Qian and Kun in the Book of Changes (Yi)? How so? In high antiquity, customs and ethos had not yet opened up, and human culture had not yet become manifest. The people all made their upper garments of grass andleaves, so the distinction between superior and inferior was unclear; they made their lower garments of feathers and skins, so the ranks of noble and base could not be distinguished. Yet as this was practiced for a long time, they grew ever more weary of it, and as it accumulated deeply, its abuses grew ever worse; they wished to change it, yet could not change it by themselves. title: 成化十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
象道襞幅為裳其色纁而象事尊卑貴賤之分
截然以明章服等威之制秩然以辨時雍之治
自爾而臻有不待於施設也文明之化自爾而
成有不待於教令也夫群聖通變無為之治如
此豈無所自哉疑有取於易之乾坤焉是故乾
者易中純陽之卦陽極於九則化而為陰其化
也有莫測其化之之迹坤者易中純陰之卦陰
極於六則變而為陽其變也有莫究其變之之
故黄帝堯舜通衣裳之變而化成俗美民不知
===
誰之為功者疑其有象于是夫豈無謂歟雖然
伏羲神農皆以聖神之德居制作之位而衣裳
之制何有待於黄帝堯舜三聖人歟蓋聖人主
化如禹之治水順則當順之治則順治之因時
而已否則古今器用以一聖人制之而有餘矣
固無待於歴世之聖人也吾夫子傳乾文言嘗
曰先天而天弗違後天而奉天時驗諸此而益
信
書義

信

punctuated:
象道，襞幅為裳，其色纁而象事。尊卑貴賤之分截然以明，章服等威之制秩然以辨。時雍之治自爾而臻，有不待於施設也；文明之化自爾而成，有不待於教令也。夫群聖通變無為之治如此，豈無所自哉？疑有取於《易》之《乾》、《坤》焉。是故《乾》者，《易》中純陽之卦，陽極於九，則化而為陰，其化也有莫測其化之之迹；《坤》者，《易》中純陰之卦，陰極於六，則變而為陽，其變也有莫究其變之之故。黄帝、堯、舜通衣裳之變，而化成俗美，民不知誰之為功者，疑其有象于是，夫豈無謂歟？雖然，伏羲、神農皆以聖神之德居制作之位，而衣裳之制何有待於黄帝、堯、舜三聖人歟？蓋聖人主化，如禹之治水，順則當順之，治則順治之，因時而已。否則，古今器用以一聖人制之而有餘矣，固無待於歴世之聖人也。吾夫子傳《乾》《文言》嘗曰：「先天而天弗違，後天而奉天時。」驗諸此而益信。

書義
translation_en:
…symbolized the Way; pleated widths of cloth formed the lower garments, and their color was light red, symbolizing affairs. The distinctions between honored and humble, noble and base were thereby made sharply clear; the regulations for insignia, robes, and graded prestige were thereby systematically differentiated. Governance of harmonious peace was thus attained of itself, without waiting for administrative measures; the transformation of civilization was thus completed of itself, without waiting for instructions and commands. Now, that the governance of the sages—comprehending change and acting through non-action—was like this: how could it have had no source? It presumably drew its inspiration from the hexagrams Qian and Kun in the Book of Changes (Yi). Therefore, Qian is the hexagram of pure yang in the Book of Changes; when yang reaches its extreme at nine, it transforms into yin, and in its transformation no one can fathom the traces of how it transforms. Kun is the hexagram of pure yin in the Book of Changes; when yin reaches its extreme at six, it changes into yang, and in its change no one can exhaustively trace the reason why it changes. The Yellow Emperor (Huangdi), Yao, and Shun comprehended the changes in upper and lower garments, so that transformation was achieved and customs became admirable, while the people did not know whose achievement it was. To surmise that they took their symbolic model from these hexagrams—how could this be said without basis? Even so, Fuxi and Shennong both occupied the position of institutional creators by virtue of their sage and spirit-like virtue; why then did the institution of upper and lower garments have to wait for the three sages, the Yellow Emperor, Yao, and Shun? This is because when a sage presides over transformation, it is like Yu's controlling the waters: where they follow a natural course, one ought to follow them, and in governing them, one governs by following their nature—simply adapting to the times. Otherwise, a single sage would have been more than sufficient to institute all implements and usages of antiquity and the present, and there would certainly have been no need to wait for sages across successive generations. Our Master Confucius, in his commentary the "Words of the Text" (Wenyan) on Qian, once said: "When he precedes Heaven, Heaven does not act in opposition to him; when he follows Heaven, he observes Heaven's timing." Tested against this, it is all the more credible.

Expositions on the Book of Documents (Shuyi)

"The Huai and Yi rivers were regulated; Mounts Meng and Yu were cultivated. The Daye Marsh was contained; the Dongyuan plain was brought to level order."

Ni Fu 倪黻

title: 成化十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
是地之髙者若蒙羽二山亦可以載耕載耘而
施種植之功載芟載柞而興樹藝之利矣若夫
徐之澤藪莫大於大野盖水之止者也昔也洪
水横流大野之波泛濫而無所止不得其治也
極矣今而濬導之力既至則大野之水蓄而復
流無復昔日泛濫之虞焉大野既治由是地之
平者若東原之地亦無卑濕之患而得底於平
無沮洳之慮而得復其舊矣吁淮沂乂而後蒙
羽藝大野豬而後東原平水土之功相因也如
===
此非大禹聖人其何能若是哉雖然大禹之功
不獨著於徐州而已觀夫九川滌源何有於淮
沂九山刋旅何有於蒙羽九澤既陂四隩既宅
又何有於大野東原也哉大禹之功於是乎不
可及矣此其所以與天地相為悠久而萬世永
賴也歟
以至于有萬邦兹惟艱哉敷求哲人俾輔
于爾後嗣制官刑儆于有位
劉繼武

是地之髙者，若蒙、羽二山，亦可以載耕載耘而施種植之功，載芟載柞而興樹藝之利矣。若夫徐之澤藪，莫大於大野，盖水之止者也。昔也洪水横流，大野之波泛濫而無所止，不得其治也極矣。今而濬導之力既至，則大野之水蓄而復流，無復昔日泛濫之虞焉。大野既治，由是地之平者，若東原之地，亦無卑濕之患而得底於平，無沮洳之慮而得復其舊矣。吁！淮、沂乂而後蒙、羽藝，大野豬而後東原平，水土之功相因也如此。非大禹聖人，其何能若是哉！雖然，大禹之功，不獨著於徐州而已。觀夫「九川滌源」，何有於淮、沂？「九山刋旅」，何有於蒙、羽？「九澤既陂，四隩既宅」，又何有於大野、東原也哉？大禹之功，於是乎不可及矣！此其所以與天地相為悠久，而萬世永賴也歟！
「以至于有萬邦，兹惟艱哉！敷求哲人，俾輔于爾後嗣。制官刑，儆于有位。」
劉繼武
translation_en:
…this, the high-lying lands, such as the two mountains Meng and Yu, could also be plowed and weeded to apply the work of planting, and cleared of grass and trees to raise the benefits of arboriculture and agriculture. As for the marshes of Xuzhou, none is greater than Daye, which is standing water. In the past, when the floodwaters flowed unchecked, the waves of Daye overflowed without anywhere to stop; its lack of control had reached an extreme. Now that the effort of dredging and channeling had been accomplished, the waters of Daye were gathered and flowed again, with no further worry of the overflowing of former days. Once Daye was brought under control, from this the flat lands, such as the land of Dongyuan, also had no affliction of low-lying dampness and were able to be brought to levelness, and had no anxiety of waterlogged mire and were able to be restored to their former state. Ah! Only after the Huai and Yi rivers were regulated were Mount Meng and Mount Yu cultivated; only after the Daye marsh was pooled was Dongyuan leveled. Such is the way the achievements of water and land depend upon one another. Were it not for the sage Great Yu, how could anyone have accomplished this? Even so, the achievements of Great Yu were not manifested in Xuzhou alone. When one observes that "the nine rivers had their sources cleared," what was there to the Huai and the Yi? When "the nine mountains were cleared of trees and sacrificed to," what was there to Meng and Yu? When "the nine marshes were banked, and the four quarters were made habitable," what more was there to Daye and Dongyuan? In this, the achievements of Great Yu cannot be equaled! Is this not why they endure as long as heaven and earth, and are relied upon forever for ten thousand generations?

"…down to coming into possession of the myriad states—this was arduous indeed! Widely sought out wise men to assist you, his descendants. He instituted punishments for officials, to warn those in office."

Liu Jiwu 劉繼武

太甲之意

甲所以克終允德也
===
聖君得天下之難也不惟求賢以輔乎後而又
立法以戒乎臣夫得天下固難保天下亦不易
也成湯之得天下既難矣得不求賢立法以為
保天下之慮哉想夫伊尹訓導太甲之意若曰
先王成湯肇脩人紀之常克盡孝敬之實是以
德日以盛業日以廣天命歸之人心戴之由七
十里而至于有萬邦自諸侯而升為天子積累
之勤茲亦難矣締造之功茲亦艱矣夫成湯之
得天下也如此其難則其慮天下而保之也豈

德日以盛業日以廣天命歸之人心戴之由七
十里而至于有萬邦自諸侯而升為天子積累
之勤玆亦難矣締造之功玆亦艱矣夫成湯之
得天下也如此其難則其慮天下而保之也豈
punctuated:
同考試官訓導戴批：連日閱卷，皆蹈襲陳腐，今人厭觀。忽得此篇，說出成湯創業裕後處，明白無蘊，刋範後學，允協輿論。
同考試官教授裘批：《伊訓》一題，場中類能作之，但繁瑣不可人意。求其簡明典實如是篇者，不多見也。

聖君得天下之難也，不惟求賢以輔乎後，而又立法以戒乎臣。夫得天下固難，保天下亦不易也。成湯之得天下既難矣，得不求賢立法以為保天下之慮哉？想夫伊尹訓導太甲之意，若曰：先王成湯，肇脩人紀之常，克盡孝敬之實，是以德日以盛，業日以廣，天命歸之，人心戴之。由七十里而至于有萬邦，自諸侯而升為天子，積累之勤，茲亦難矣；締造之功，茲亦艱矣。夫成湯之得天下也如此其難，則其慮天下而保之也，豈
translation_en:
Associate Examiner and Assistant Instructor Dai's comment: For several days of reading papers, they have all followed stale clichés, making one tired of looking at them [reading 今 as 令]. Suddenly obtaining this essay, which explains how Cheng Tang founded the dynastic enterprise and enriched his posterity with utter clarity and nothing left obscure, to be carved as a model for later scholars, it truly accords with public opinion.
Associate Examiner and Instructor Qiu's comment: On this topic from the "Instructions of Yi" (Yi xun), candidates in the examination hall are generally able to compose essays, yet they are tedious and unsatisfactory. To seek one as concise, clear, and classically grounded as this essay—such is rarely seen.
Examiner and Reader-in-Waiting Zhou's comment: The writing is detailed and well-ordered, capturing the intent of Yi Yin's exhortation and warning to Tai Jia.
Examiner and Left Mentor Liu's comment: Yi Yin's words were as sincere and earnest as this; this is how Tai Jia was able in the end to be of sincere virtue.
In the difficulty with which the sage ruler gained the realm, he not only sought worthy men to assist his successors, but also established laws to warn his ministers. Now, gaining the realm is certainly difficult, and preserving the realm is also not easy. Since Cheng Tang's gaining of the realm was already so difficult, how could he not seek worthy men and establish laws as a plan for preserving the realm? One may imagine the intent of Yi Yin in instructing and guiding Tai Jia, as if to say: The Former King Cheng Tang first cultivated the constant norms of human relationships and was able to fulfill the reality of filial piety and reverence. Therefore, his virtue grew more flourishing by the day and his enterprise grew broader by the day; the Mandate of Heaven turned to him, and the hearts of the people supported him. From a territory of seventy li he came to possess the myriad states, and from a feudal lord he rose to become the Son of Heaven. The toil of accumulation—this indeed was difficult! The merit of founding and constructing—this indeed was arduous! Since Cheng Tang's gaining of the realm was as difficult as this, when he took thought for the realm so as to preserve it, how…

… be willing to treat it lightly and leave it at that? Therefore, worthy talents are the foundation for assisting in governance: he surely sought out worthy and wise gentlemen widely, and recruited outstanding and capable men from all sides to place them in the various official positions, so that they would assist on the left and right to support you, his successor, and offer instruction morning and evening to enlighten you, his descendant, thereby carrying on the dynastic line without end. Laws and ordinances are the instruments for assisting in governance: he surely instituted the penal rules for officialdom, setting them forth as instructions against decadent faults to warn those in office, so that they would know what to guard against and all rectify what their ruler failed to reach, and know what to fear and be cautious about and all amend where their ruler fell short, thereby preserving the foundational enterprise without limit. Ah! Such was the difficulty with which Tang the Successful gained the empire and the far-sightedness with which he planned for the empire. When Yi Yin cited these things to inform Tai Jia, how deep was his loyal and loving intention! If we examine Tai Jia, at another time he ruined the norms through his desires and ruined propriety through his self-indulgence; regarding the difficulty of the former king's founding of the enterprise and his concern for handing down the line, he was indeed ignorant and unaware. Yi Yin foresaw the subtle signs of this, and therefore at the very beginning of his succession to the throne, he earnestly spoke of it in advance, and in the text that follows he repeatedly admonished him further with the fortune and misfortune of Heaven's Mandate and human affairs—this can truly be called urgent and thorough. Afterward, Tai Jia was indeed able to bring his sincere virtue to completion and become an admirable ruler of the Shang; who could say it was not due to the strength of Yi Yin's instruction and guidance?

Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor Huang 黃: Most writers refer to the Minister of Education (situ 司徒) as a Grand Master (dafu 大夫) and treat clothing and food as a parallel pair in their exposition, completely missing the meaning of the commentary. This essay alone is able to depict the sentiment of boundless love for the worthy so vividly that it seems right before one’s eyes. Moreover, its phrasing is concise and apt; compared to it, other compositions are left far behind staring in the dust. It deserves a high ranking.
Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor Zhao 趙: This topic expresses a single idea through repeated phrasing, so the test lies in how one handles the remaining words [?]; in the examination hall, essays are either verbose or sketchy. This composition is concise in wording and clear in meaning, like a fine steed taking the bridle whose spirited vigor simply cannot be held back.
Comment by Examiner Reader-in-waiting Zhou 周: Master Cheng (Chengzi 程子) said: “The meaning of boundless love for the worthy should be seen in the two phrases ‘when worn out, I [will]’ (bi yu 敝予) and ‘when returning, I [will]’ (huan yu 還予).” This composition grasps it.
Comment by Examiner Left Mentor Liu 劉: Nuanced and thorough, it captures the intention of the poet.

The people of Zhou repeatedly praised the robes of the Minister of Education, thereby expressing an unending affection for him. Now, the robes in themselves are not what is worthy of praise; it is only that out of affection for the Minister of Education, their feelings extended even to his robes. When their affection for him reached such an unending degree, how great must the worthiness of the Minister of Education have been! Duke Huan of Zheng (Zheng Huan gong 鄭桓公) and Duke Wu (Wu gong 武公) successively served as Minister of Education for Zhou; the people of Zhou loved them and composed this ode. When I imagine the sentiment of their affection, it is as if they were saying: The Minister of Education is a minister of the royal court, and the black robe is the vestment of a royal minister. Only our Duke Huan [of Zheng] could cultivate his duties as a royal minister, so that wearing these robes was most fitting; and when it came to our Duke Wu, he did not disgrace his father's virtue, so that wearing these garments was most suitable. Since the robes are so fitting, should they become worn out, we will make new ones for him, so that these robes remain ever fine; since the garments are so suitable, should they become old, we will replace them for him, so that these garments remain ever new. Yet to replace his garments without visiting him in person would border on disrespect, and so we go again to the lodging where he resides; and to go to his lodging without offering a gift would border on negligence, and so when he returns we present him with fine grain. The feelings of the people of Zhou may indeed be called generous! Yet they must repeat their words a second time, saying: "How fine are the black robes the Duke wears! When they are worn out, how could we not remake them for him? Not only this, we shall wait upon the Duke at his private court to draw near to the splendor of his morality; and when he returns, we shall again present him with fine grain, hoping thereby to fulfill our hearts' devotion." The feelings of the people of Zhou may indeed be called earnest! Yet they must repeat their words a third time, saying: "How grand are the black robes the Duke wears! When they are worn out, how could we not make them anew for him? Not only so, we shall pay our respects to the Duke in his private residence to behold the model of his propriety and righteousness; and when he returns, we shall again offer him fine grain, hoping thereby to exhaust our sincerity." Alas! With an endless affection and love expressed in repeated and varied words, how supreme was the devotion of the people of Zhou toward Dukes Huan and Wu! … [that the scholars of the Zhou capital spoke with] patterned refinement can be seen right here. That this is what is called the lingering grace of the former kings—how is that not true indeed!

"What is most powerful is being a true man; the four quarters take it as their precept. What is most illustrious is virtue; the hundred lords take it as their model." [Classic of Poetry, Ode 269, "Lie wen"]

Tang Qin 唐欽

Only this piece deeply accords with the meaning of the topic, excelling in both diction and principle; it is indeed an outstanding specimen among the papers on the Classic of Poetry (Pajing). What shame could there be in recommending him for the list?

Examiner and Left Mentor of the Secretariat of the Heir Apparent Liu 劉 comments: The King of Zhou's intention in admonishing and encouraging the feudal lords can be vividly seen here.

When the Way of Man is strong, there is none in the world who does not take it as a model; when the virtue of the ruler is manifest, there is none among the feudal lords who does not take it as a model. Now the Way and virtue are principles shared by all human hearts. When one perfects the Way and virtue within oneself and carries moral transformation to its utmost among others, how can that whereby one is strong and illustrious not be seen? Of old, when the King of Zhou presented the wine-offering to the feudal lords who assisted at the sacrifice, he admonished and encouraged them, as if to say: In the world there are majesty and might—who among men does not call them strong? Yet there is that which does not rely upon majesty and does not trouble with…

title: 成化十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
力而強莫強之者維人道乎誠於人道焉是盡
則五品之倫無不正萬事之理無不立由是雖
無心於人之訓也而嵎夷之西昧谷之東莫不
於我乎是訓矣雖無意於人之法也而南交之
北朔方之南莫不於我乎是法矣然則人道之
強也何如哉若夫天下有勢位焉人孰不謂之
顯然有不假乎勢不賴乎位而顯莫顯之者維
君德乎誠於君德焉是脩則仁義禮智之性于
以全脩齊治平之道于以具由是自侯甸以至
===
于綏要荒九州之國何遠也而德吾德者不以
遠而或殊自公侯以至于伯子男四國之君何
衆也而心吾心者不以衆而或間然則君德之
顯也何如哉吁王者告戒諸侯而形之咏歌如
此則當時諸侯豈有不惕然感動而惟道德之
是勉乎雖然有周盛時賢才衆多若藩屏王室
皇皇宜君者有焉肅肅助祭者有焉人道君德
宜無不備矣而王者猶必戒勉之拳拳何哉盖
怠荒宴豫之心常生於功烈盛滿之日雖虞庭

怠荒宴豫之心常生於功烈盛滿之日雖虞庭
punctuated: 力，而強莫強之者，維人道乎！誠於人道焉是盡，則五品之倫無不正，萬事之理無不立。由是雖無心於人之訓也，而嵎夷之西、昧谷之東，莫不於我乎是訓矣；雖無意於人之法也，而南交之北、朔方之南，莫不於我乎是法矣。然則人道之強也何如哉！若夫天下有勢位焉，人孰不謂之顯？然有不假乎勢、不賴乎位，而顯莫顯之者，維君德乎！誠於君德焉是脩，則仁義禮智之性于以全，脩齊治平之道于以具。由是自侯、甸以至于綏、要、荒，九州之國何遠也，而德吾德者，不以遠而或殊；自公、侯以至于伯、子、男，四國之君何衆也，而心吾心者，不以衆而或間。然則君德之顯也何如哉！吁！王者告戒諸侯，而形之咏歌如此，則當時諸侯，豈有不惕然感動，而惟道德之是勉乎？雖然，有周盛時，賢才衆多，若藩屏王室，皇皇宜君者有焉，肅肅助祭者有焉，人道、君德，宜無不備矣。而王者猶必戒勉之拳拳，何哉？盖怠荒宴豫之心，常生於功烈盛滿之日，雖虞庭…
translation_en:
…force, and yet nothing is stronger than this—is it not the Way of Man! If one truly exhausts the Way of Man, then none of the five human relationships will fail to be rectified, and none of the principles of the myriad affairs will fail to be established. Thereby, even though one has no intention of instructing others, from west of Yuyi to east of Meigu, there are none who do not take instruction from us; even though one has no deliberate thought of serving as a model for others, from north of Nanjiao to south of Shuofang, there are none who do not take us as their model. How great, then, is the strength of the Way of Man!

As for possessing power and position in the world, who does not call that illustrious? Yet there is that which neither borrows from power nor relies on position, and nothing is more illustrious than it—is it not the virtue of a ruler! If one truly cultivates the virtue of a ruler, then the nature of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom is thereby made complete, and the principles of self-cultivation, regulating the family, governing the state, and bringing peace to the world are thereby fully provided. Consequently, from the Royal and Princely Domains out to the Pacified, Controlled, and Wild Domains, how distant are the states of the Nine Provinces! Yet those who make our virtue their own virtue do not differ on account of distance. From dukes and marquises down to earls, viscounts, and barons, how numerous are the rulers of the four quarters! Yet those who make our mind their own mind are not divided on account of their multitude. How great, then, is the illustriousness of the ruler's virtue!

Ah! When the true king admonished and encouraged the feudal lords and gave it expression in song like this, how could the feudal lords of that time fail to be awestruck and moved to exert themselves solely in the Way and in virtue? Even so, in the flourishing era of the Zhou, worthy talents were numerous: among those who served as screens and bulwarks for the royal house, there were those who were splendid and fitted to be rulers, and there were those who reverently assisted at the sacrifices; the Way of Man and the virtue of a ruler ought to have been completely present in them. Why, then, did the king still have to admonish and encourage them with such earnestness? It is because minds given to indolence, neglect, ease, and pleasure constantly arise in days when merits and achievements are at their height; even in the court of Yu…

text:

熈泰和之盛而非後世之所及也歟

春秋義

同考試官教授羅批：此卷七篇，文理通暢，講貫明白。是篇尤能發揮聖人憂世之意，深合傳義，宜在所取。

考試官左庶子劉批：發明王伯、夷夏之消長，非他卷所及。

大國謀内以圖伯，《春秋》既為王道慮；外夷猾夏以爭強，《春秋》復為中國憂。此齊桓次師于郎，荊楚敗蔡于莘，《春秋》備書，而王伯、夷夏之消長見矣。慨夫王道流行，侯伯受職，未聞有圖伯者也。今也，齊桓偕宋人之師，為于郎之次，將以謀魯，以圖伯於果。當是時也，魯無可聲之罪、致師之
translation_en:
… ruler and ministers also spoke of "maintaining vigilance when there is no cause for anxiety." Alas! Is this not how they achieved the flourishing height of harmonious peace, something that later generations could never match?

Exposition on the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu)
"The army of Qi and the army of Song halted at Lang." "Jing [Chu] defeated the army of Cai at Shen, and returned home with Xianwu, Marquis of Cai." (Both from the tenth year of Duke Zhuang.)
By Cheng Zhen
Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor Luo: The seven essays in this examination paper are coherent in argument and clear in exposition. This piece is especially able to bring out the Sage's concern for the world; it deeply accords with the meaning of the commentaries and deserves to be selected.
Comment by Examiner Academician Reader-in-waiting Zhou: Hegemonic ambitions and barbarian calamities both began in this year of Duke Zhuang of Lu, and the Spring and Autumn Annals laments this. This composition develops the theme very thoroughly.
Comment by Examiner Left Mentor Liu: It elucidates the waxing and waning of the Kingly Way versus hegemony, and of the barbarians versus the central states, in a manner that other papers cannot match.

When a great state plots within the realm to seek hegemony, the Spring and Autumn Annals is concerned for the Kingly Way; when outer barbarians disturb the central states (Xia) to contend for supremacy, the Spring and Autumn Annals further worries for the Central States. Thus, when Duke Huan of Qi halted his army at Lang, and when Jing-Chu defeated Cai at Shen, the Spring and Autumn Annals recorded both in full, and the waxing and waning of the Kingly Way and hegemony, of barbarians and the central states, became manifest. Alas, when the Kingly Way prevailed, the feudal lords and regional earls received their appointed duties, and one never heard of anyone plotting for hegemony. Now, however, Duke Huan of Qi, together with the army of the men of Song, made this halt at Lang, intending to plot against Lu in order to carry through [?] his quest for hegemony. At that time, Lu had no crime that could be openly denounced, nor any cause to provoke an expedition…

title: 成化十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
由齊桓何為而次師于郎耶誠以魯為人望之
國秉禮之邦諸侯所觀望而從違者也不得魯
不可以集事是以按兵不進駐師不前欲脅之
以從已焉夫魯為周公之後而所遇如此則伯
主之聲燄自是而日著文武之恩澤自是而日
泯矣春秋得不為王道慮乎若夫周室未衰荆
楚帖服未聞有争強者也今也楚人因息媯之
故舉虐蔡之兵遂執蔡以争強於南當是時也
蔡無致釁之由取伐之道楚人何為而加兵於
===
蔡耶誠以蔡為要領之國喉襟之地諸侯所恃
以為藩表者也不敗蔡則不可以窺内是以敗
衂其師執辱其君欲藉之以為援焉夫蔡為文
昭之裔而所遇如此則蛇豕之毒自是而浸長
諸姬之國自是而靡寧矣春秋得不為中國憂
乎吁天下無王者齊為之也天下無中國者楚
為之也春秋傷世變之大而致謹於齊楚夫豈
無意哉抑又考之王者不作而後齊晋興茍有
王者作則文武之業可興而齊晋息矣伯者不

punctuated: 由，齊桓何為而次師于郎耶？誠以魯為人望之國、秉禮之邦，諸侯所觀望而從違者也。不得魯，不可以集事，是以按兵不進，駐師不前，欲脅之以從已焉。夫魯為周公之後，而所遇如此，則伯主之聲燄自是而日著，文、武之恩澤自是而日泯矣，《春秋》得不為王道慮乎？若夫周室未衰，荆楚帖服，未聞有争強者也。今也楚人因息媯之故，舉虐蔡之兵，遂執蔡以争強於南。當是時也，蔡無致釁之由、取伐之道，楚人何為而加兵於蔡耶？誠以蔡為要領之國、喉襟之地，諸侯所恃以為藩表者也。不敗蔡，則不可以窺内，是以敗衂其師，執辱其君，欲藉之以為援焉。夫蔡為文昭之裔，而所遇如此，則蛇豕之毒自是而浸長，諸姬之國自是而靡寧矣，《春秋》得不為中國憂乎？吁！天下無王者，齊為之也；天下無中國者，楚為之也。《春秋》傷世變之大，而致謹於齊、楚，夫豈無意哉！抑又考之，王者不作而後齊、晋興；茍有王者作，則文、武之業可興，而齊、晋息矣。伯者不
translation_en: … cause [to provoke an attack], why then did Duke Huan of Qi halt his troops at Lang? Truly it was because Lu was a state looked up to by men and a polity that upheld the rites, one upon which the feudal lords watched to decide whether to follow or turn away. Without winning over Lu, he could not accomplish his enterprise; therefore he held back his forces without advancing and stationed his army without moving forward, wishing to coerce Lu into following him. Now, Lu was the descendant of the Duke of Zhou, and yet what it met with was such as this; thus the prestige and blaze of the hegemonic rulers grew more manifest day by day from this point on, while the grace and beneficence of Kings Wen and Wu faded away day by day from this point on. Could the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) help but be anxious for the Kingly Way? As for when the house of Zhou had not yet declined, Jing-Chu was submissive and obedient, and one had not heard of anyone contending for supremacy. Now, however, because of Xi Gui, the men of Chu raised an army to ravage Cai, and thereupon seized [the Marquis of] Cai in order to contend for supremacy in the south. At that time, Cai had given no cause to provoke a feud and had pursued no course to invite a punitive expedition; why then did the men of Chu inflict armed force upon Cai? Truly it was because Cai was a state at a vital nexus, a territory of throat and collar, upon which the feudal lords relied as an outer bulwark. Without defeating Cai, Chu could not peer into the interior; therefore it routed and crushed Cai's army and seized and humiliated its ruler, wishing to use Cai as a support. Now, Cai was the descendant of the luminous line of King Wen (Wenzhao), and yet what it met with was such as this; thus the venom of serpents and swine gradually grew from this point on, and the states of the Ji clan had no peace from this point on. Could the Spring and Autumn Annals help but worry for the Central States? Alas! That the realm had no True King was the doing of Qi; that the realm had no Central States was the doing of Chu. When the Spring and Autumn Annals lamented the magnitude of the world's transformations and exercised special care with regard to Qi and Chu, how could it have been without intent!
