title: 成化十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
故齊桓主伯仗尊王之大義講于幽之再盟斯
時也若宋若魯皆從事載書而罔敢差池若陳
若鄭皆奔走牲歃而罔敢違越內外大小翕然
来同此齊伯之方盛故春秋美其績特書曰同
盟以予之也若夫晋靈主伯因諸侯之外楚講
新城之同盟斯時也從楚諸侯改轍而来同輔
外友邦執圭而在列諸侯之散者復合此晋伯
之漸衰故春秋致其意亦書曰同盟以予之也
至於晋景主伯復因討貳之役同講清丘之盟
===
===
斯時也諸侯之叛晋者紛紛而勉從外楚之舉
列國之從晋者落落而強為同盟之歃異者衆
而同者鮮晋不復可言伯矣而春秋猶以同盟
書者盖嘉其不以勝負為從違舍燎原強盛之
楚從喪敗方新之晋是故猶以同盟許之然曰
視新城之役且不能及于幽之盟又安可同日
而語哉愚故曰即人心之合散見伯業之盛衰
者其以是夫大抵自于幽觀新城則于幽盛之
始而新城衰之始也自新城觀清丘則新城衰

至於晉景主伯復因討貳之役同講清丘之盟

列國之從晉者落落而強為同盟之歃異者衆
而同者鮮晉不復可言伯矣而春秋猶以同盟

楚從喪敗方新之晉是故猶以同盟許之然田

而語哉愚故曰即人心之合散見伯業之盛衰

始而新城衰之始也自新城觀清丘則新城衰
punctuated: 故齊桓主伯，仗尊王之大義，講于幽之再盟。斯時也，若宋若魯，皆從事載書而罔敢差池；若陳若鄭，皆奔走牲歃而罔敢違越。內外大小，翕然来同，此齊伯之方盛，故《春秋》美其績，特書曰「同盟」以予之也。若夫晋靈主伯，因諸侯之外楚，講新城之同盟。斯時也，從楚諸侯改轍而来同，輔外友邦執圭而在列，諸侯之散者復合，此晋伯之漸衰，故《春秋》致其意，亦書曰「同盟」以予之也。至於晋景主伯，復因討貳之役，同講清丘之盟。斯時也，諸侯之叛晋者紛紛，而勉從外楚之舉；列國之從晋者落落，而強為同盟之歃。異者衆而同者鮮，晋不復可言伯矣。而《春秋》猶以「同盟」書者，盖嘉其不以勝負為從違，舍燎原強盛之楚，從喪敗方新之晋，是故猶以「同盟」許之。然曰視新城之役且不能及，于幽之盟又安可同日而語哉！愚故曰：即人心之合散，見伯業之盛衰者，其以是夫！大抵自于幽觀新城，則于幽盛之始，而新城衰之始也；自新城觀清丘，則新城衰…
translation_en:
…for this reason, when Duke Huan of Qi presided over the hegemony, he relied on the great righteousness of honoring the King to convene the second covenant at You. At that time, states such as Song and Lu all attended to the covenant text and none dared to falter; states such as Chen and Zheng all hastened to the sacrificial blood-smearing and none dared to transgress. States inner and outer, great and small, came together in harmony to join the pact. This was when the hegemony of Qi was at its height; therefore the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) praised its achievement and specially recorded it as a "joint covenant" (tongmeng) in order to commend it.

As for when Duke Ling of Jin presided over the hegemony, taking advantage of the feudal lords' rejection of Chu, he convened the joint covenant at Xincheng. At that time, the feudal lords who had followed Chu changed course and came to join; allied states that assisted against the outsider held their jade tablets and took their places in the ranks. The feudal lords who had been scattered were reunited. This was when the hegemony of Jin was gradually declining; therefore the Spring and Autumn Annals conveyed its sentiment and likewise recorded it as a "joint covenant" in order to commend it.

When it came to Duke Jing of Jin presiding over the hegemony, once again on account of a campaign to punish disaffection, they jointly convened the covenant at Qingqiu. At that time, the feudal lords rebelling against Jin were numerous, and only reluctantly followed the initiative to exclude Chu; the various states following Jin were few and far between, and only under compulsion performed the blood-smearing of the joint covenant. Those at variance were many while those in accord were few; Jin could no longer be spoken of as hegemon. Yet the reason the Spring and Autumn Annals still recorded it as a "joint covenant" was that it praised them for not basing their allegiance or defection on victory or defeat—abandoning Chu, which was strong and flourishing like a prairie fire, and following Jin, which had just suffered a fresh defeat. For this reason it still granted them the term "joint covenant." Yet if even compared to the campaign of Xincheng it could not measure up, how could it be spoken of in the same breath as the covenant at You!

I therefore say: observing the rise and decline of hegemonic rule from the coming together and scattering of people's hearts—is it not on this account! On the whole, if one views Xincheng from the perspective of You, then You was the beginning of flourishing, while Xincheng was the beginning of decline; if one views Qingqiu from the perspective of Xincheng, then Xincheng was the [beginning of] decline…

title: 成化十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
居之無法而使之失所則何以致其向義而立
學以教之哉王制記此謂夫有土不可以無民
有民不可以無居先王於此果何如哉誠以邑
以地制地之多寡未易知也必量其所容而四
井之邑制焉民以地居地之長短未易見也必
度其所至而萬井之民居焉然地也邑也必相
其宜以制之不多寡之有偏可也邑也居也必
量其稱以居之不長短之有失可也地邑民居
既參相得由是田必事農而閑曠之土無矣人
===
必授田而游惰之民鮮矣食焉有度而無不足
之患事焉以時而無不及之務居民之道如此
則天下之民豈有不安其居者哉民居既安殆
見役之則樂其事而不至勞苦也動之則勸其
功而不由勉強也知君之當尊尊之而有遜志
知上之當親親之而無離心夫如是則禮義之
心萌矣于焉設為學校而使之有以明乎善干
焉建立庠序而教之有以復其性吁先王之於
民不惟居之而又教之如此宜其治化之盛而

punctuated: 居之無法，而使之失所，則何以致其向義而立學以教之哉？《王制》記此，謂夫有土不可以無民，有民不可以無居，先王於此果何如哉？誠以邑以地制，地之多寡未易知也，必量其所容，而四井之邑制焉；民以地居，地之長短未易見也，必度其所至，而萬井之民居焉。然地也、邑也，必相其宜以制之，不多寡之有偏可也；邑也、居也，必量其稱以居之，不長短之有失可也。地、邑、民居，既參相得，由是田必事農，而閑曠之土無矣；人必授田，而游惰之民鮮矣。食焉有度，而無不足之患；事焉以時，而無不及之務。居民之道如此，則天下之民豈有不安其居者哉？民居既安，殆見役之則樂其事，而不至勞苦也；動之則勸其功，而不由勉強也。知君之當尊，尊之而有遜志；知上之當親，親之而無離心。夫如是，則禮義之心萌矣。于焉設為學校，而使之有以明乎善；干焉建立庠序，而教之有以復其性。吁！先王之於民，不惟居之而又教之如此，宜其治化之盛，而
translation_en:
…there is no proper method for settling them, thereby causing them to lose their livelihood, then how could one bring them to incline toward righteousness and establish schools to instruct them?

When the "Royal Regulations" (Wangzhi) chapter records this, it means that where there is territory there cannot be a lack of people, and where there are people there cannot be a lack of settlements. How, then, did the former kings handle this? Truly, because townships are laid out according to the land, and the abundance or scarcity of the land is not easily known, one must measure what it can hold, and thus townships of four well-fields are established. Because the people are settled according to the land, and the extent of the land is not easily seen, one must survey how far it reaches, and thus the people of ten thousand well-fields are settled. Yet as for the land and the townships, one must examine what is suitable in order to lay them out, so that there is no imbalance of too much or too little; as for the townships and the settlements, one must measure their correspondence in order to settle them, so that there is no discrepancy in extent.

Once land, townships, and the people's settlements are mutually proportioned in all three respects, every field is devoted to farming and there is no idle, uncultivated land; every person is allotted a field and there are few wandering, indolent people. Consumption is regulated by measure, so there is no worry of insufficiency; labor is employed according to the seasons, so there are no tasks left unaccomplished. When the way of settling the people is like this, how could there be any people in the world who are not secure in their dwellings?

Once the people's dwellings are secure, one will find that when they are conscripted for service, they take pleasure in their work and do not feel worn down by hardship; when they are mobilized, they encourage one another in their achievements and do not act out of compulsion. Knowing that the ruler ought to be revered, they revere him with a compliant will; knowing that superiors ought to be held dear, they hold them dear without a divided heart. When it is like this, a sense of ritual and righteousness begins to sprout. Thereupon schools (xuexiao) are instituted to enable them to understand the good; thereupon local academies (xiangxu) are established to instruct them so that they may recover their innate nature.

Ah! In dealing with the people, the former kings not only settled them, but also instructed them in this manner. Fitting indeed that the flourishing of their governance and moral transformation…

title: 成化十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
非後世之所及也歟抑又論之人形天地之氣
而性天地之理其尊君親上盖其良心也獨安
養不足而禮義不興由是良心陷溺而為非耳
聖人制為安養之術禮義之教則民之陷溺者
皆可化而為善所謂裁成天地之道此之謂歟
故聖人耐以天下為一家以中國為一人
者非意之也必知其情辟於其義明於其
利達於其患然後能為之
姜溥

translation_en:
… beyond what later ages could attain! Furthermore, to discuss this further: human beings take their bodily form from the vital force (qi) of Heaven and Earth, and their human nature from the principle (li) of Heaven and Earth. Their honoring the ruler and feeling affection for their superiors stems from their innate good conscience. It is only when peaceful nourishment is insufficient and ritual and righteousness do not flourish that this good conscience becomes submerged and people do wrong. When the sages institute methods of peaceful nourishment and teachings of ritual and righteousness, then those among the people who have fallen into error can all be transformed toward goodness. Does not the saying "regulating and completing the Way of Heaven and Earth" refer to just this?

"Therefore, that the sage is able to regard All under Heaven as one family, and the Central States as one person, is not something done by mere subjective conjecture. He must know their feelings, open the way to what is righteous for them, be clear about what is beneficial to them, and comprehend what is harmful to them; only then is he able to accomplish it."
Jiang Pu 姜溥
Associate Examiner Instructor Lin 林 comments: The topic is inherently grand and dignified, yet in the examination hall most candidates did not realize that human feelings are the central weight of the passage, making their structural divisions unclear. Only this essay elucidates the meaning concisely and aptly, encompassing everything without omission. He is a towering figure among the Book of Rites (Liji) candidates; what shame could there be in selecting it for the record?
Examiner Reader-in-waiting Zhou 周 comments: Taking accordance with human feelings as the essential key by which the sage achieves good governance—this grasps the main purport.
Examiner Left Mentor Liu 劉 comments: Both the diction and the reasoning are well-ordered. Among all the papers on the Classic of Rites, this piece is the finest.

That the sage is able to achieve the governance of great unification does not stem from private conjecture, for there is an essential key to it. Indeed, in governing All under Heaven, nothing is more essential than human feelings. When the sage accords with human feelings and does not rely on his own…

title: 成化十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
私則豈不能大一統之治也哉且夫一統之盛
固聖人之所欲盛治之成則聖人之能事是故
井聚廬分天下之家非一家也聖人能合天下
之異而歸諸同與一家也不殊肩摩車擊中國
之人非一人也聖人能會中國之衆而合于一
與一人也無間夫聖人之所以能一天下中國
者豈私意億度之哉亦惟因人情為之而已喜
怒哀懼愛惡欲者人之情也聖人能知其情故
不拂其好惡焉是故人情所好莫好於義也則
===
===
闢其十義之途使天下中國之人皆知義所當
行而莫不由於義焉人情所欲者莫欲於利也
則達夫人利之域使天下中國之人皆知利之
所在而莫不趨於利焉至若爭奪相殺人之患
也人之所惡莫甚於此則又明示其患之所在
使皆知所避而不至相害焉夫如是吾見天下
雖非一家也而遂其由義趨利之情者猶一家
中國雖非一人也而遂其趨利避患之情者猶
一人聖人之能事至是畢矣愚故謂聖人能大

translation_en:
… selfishness, then how could he not achieve the governance of a grand unity? Moreover, the flourishing of unity is certainly what the sage desires, and the accomplishment of flourishing governance is the proper business of the sage. Therefore, with wells gathered and dwellings divided, the families of the world are not a single family; yet the sage is able to bring together the differences of the world and return them to sameness, no different from a single family. With shoulders rubbing and wheel-hubs clashing, the people of the Central States are not a single person; yet the sage is able to assemble the multitude of the Central States and unite them as one, with no gap separating them from being a single person. Now, as for that by which the sage is able to unify the world and the Central States, how could he do it through selfish intentions and conjecture? He simply acts in accordance with human feelings, and nothing more.

Joy, anger, sorrow, fear, love, aversion, and desire are the feelings of human beings. The sage is able to know their feelings, and therefore does not go against their likes and dislikes. Thus, among what human feelings like, nothing is liked more than human righteousness (yi); so he opens up the path of the ten duties of righteousness, causing the people of the world and the Central States all to know the righteousness that ought to be practiced, so that none fail to follow righteousness. Among what human feelings desire, nothing is desired more than benefit (li); so he leads them to the realm of human benefit, causing the people of the world and the Central States all to know where benefit lies, so that none fail to hasten toward benefit. As for contention, seizure, and mutual slaughter, these are human calamities, and among what people detest, nothing is worse than these; so he further clearly shows where such calamities lie, causing everyone to know what to avoid so that they do not come to harm one another.

Being thus, I see that although the world is not a single family, in fulfilling their feelings of following righteousness and hastening toward benefit, it is like a single family; and although the Central States are not a single person, in fulfilling their feelings of hastening toward benefit and avoiding calamity, they are like a single person. The proper business of the sage is herewith complete. I therefore say that the sage is able to magnify …

title: 成化十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
一統之治不由於私而有其要焉不其信歟雖
然一統之治固由乎情而治情之具又在乎禮
有禮以治之則義利由之生而患息矣禮苟廢
焉則患由之起而義利亡矣是知禮者又聖人
所以維持天下之大柄也

論
曾子之學專用心情內

translation_en:
… governance of great unity does not stem from private partiality, and possesses its essential principle—is this not truly credible? Even so, while the governance of great unity indeed depends upon human feelings, the instrument for governing feelings lies in ritual propriety. When there is ritual propriety to govern them, righteousness and benefit arise from it and calamities cease; if ritual propriety is abandoned, calamities arise from this and righteousness and benefit perish. Thus we know that ritual propriety is, furthermore, the great handle by which the sage sustains All under Heaven.

Second Session
Discourse
"Master Zeng's learning was devoted exclusively to applying the mind within" [? 心情內 for 心於內]
By Xiao Rui 蕭銳

Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor Ma 馬: In explaining principles, this essay traces beginnings and sums up ends; in phrasing, it transforms the worn-out into the new. It has clear order and structural cohesion, all flowing straight from the breast—how could one regard it as ordinary examination-hall writing? Recording it to show to others is altogether fitting.

Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor Li 李: The purport of the topic takes recovering human nature as its main theme, while the effort of practice lies in knowledge and action. Writers often set forth vague generalizations, quite lacking any ultimate grounding. This essay shows intimate personal realization and a well-ordered tone and style, expounding the essentials of Master Zeng's transmission of the Way. Most commendable, most commendable!

Comment by Examiner Academician Reader-in-Waiting Zhou 周: Nowadays candidates compete in flowery and ornate learning, prizing the险怪 (bizarre and eccentric) in their diction as something extraordinary—this is what Ouyang Yongshu 歐陽永叔 (Ouyang Xiu 歐陽修) deeply abhorred. Therefore, we have had this balanced and upright discourse engraved to serve as a standard for them.

title: 成化十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
考試官左庶子劉批論曾子之學本于心身
有源委有發越殆必有所見者也
論曰人非聖人不可以不學學非專用心於內
不可謂善學何也夫人之學所以學為聖人也
學不專用心於內以聖人為歸與不學者等耳
安在其為善學也惟專用心於內一本之心身
不至聖人之域不止焉則為善學此曾子之學
所以異於眾人而不可及歟先儒謝氏謂曾子
之學專用心於內愚請繹其說夫天之生人均
===
成之以形賦之以性初無彼此厚薄之殊但形
之成也本乎氣質氣有清濁質有美惡而不能
皆全乎是性此智愚賢不肖所由分焉彼氣之
極清質之極美心之知自與性會身之行自與
性合無所間隔不待勉强所謂聖人者固有不
待乎學矣自是而下則清濁美惡有多寡而智
愚賢不肖有等差氣質既偏物欲易蔽非學則
不能復其初也學之道柰何澄其濁汰其惡勉
而知勉而行以復乎是性之初如聖人而已矣

punctuated:
考試官左庶子劉批：論曾子之學本于心身，有源委，有發越，殆必有所見者也。

論曰：人非聖人，不可以不學；學非專用心於內，不可謂善學。何也？夫人之學，所以學為聖人也。學不專用心於內，以聖人為歸，與不學者等耳，安在其為善學也？惟專用心於內，一本之心身，不至聖人之域不止焉，則為善學。此曾子之學所以異於眾人而不可及歟！先儒謝氏謂「曾子之學，專用心於內」，愚請繹其說。夫天之生人，均成之以形，賦之以性，初無彼此厚薄之殊。但形之成也，本乎氣質；氣有清濁，質有美惡，而不能皆全乎是性，此智愚賢不肖所由分焉。彼氣之極清、質之極美，心之知自與性會，身之行自與性合，無所間隔，不待勉强，所謂聖人者，固有不待乎學矣。自是而下，則清濁美惡有多寡，而智愚賢不肖有等差。氣質既偏，物欲易蔽，非學則不能復其初也。學之道柰何？澄其濁，汰其惡，勉而知，勉而行，以復乎是性之初，如聖人而已矣。
translation_en:
Examiner Liu, Left Mentor of the Left Spring Quarters, comments: In discussing how Zengzi's learning is rooted in the mind and body, this essay traces the origins and developments and displays spirited insight; its author must surely be someone of genuine understanding.

[Topic: "Zengzi's learning was devoted exclusively to applying the mind inwardly."]
The discourse begins: Anyone who is not a sage cannot do without learning; and learning that does not consist in exclusively applying the mind inwardly cannot be called good learning. Why is this? Human learning is the means by which one learns to become a sage. If in learning one does not exclusively apply the mind inwardly and take sagehood as one's ultimate goal, it is no different from not learning at all—how could that be considered good learning? Only when one exclusively applies the mind inwardly, rooting everything in the mind and body and never stopping until the realm of the sage is reached, can it be called good learning. Is this not why the learning of Zengzi (曾子) differed from that of the multitude and could not be matched! The former Confucian scholar Master Xie (謝氏, Xie Liangzuo 謝良佐) said, "Zengzi's learning was devoted exclusively to applying the mind inwardly." I beg leave to unfold his meaning.

When Heaven gives birth to human beings, it equally forms them with physical shape and endows them with moral nature; originally there is no difference of thick or thin between one person and another. Yet the formation of physical shape is grounded in psychophysical stuff (qizhi): the vital breath (qi) may be clear or turbid, and the physical substance (zhi) may be fine or coarse, so that not everyone can preserve this moral nature in its entirety. This is whereby the wise and the foolish, the worthy and the unworthy are differentiated. In the case of one whose vital breath is supremely clear and whose physical substance is supremely fine, the knowledge of his mind naturally converges with his moral nature, and the conduct of his body naturally accords with his moral nature, without any barrier and without need of forced effort—such a person, whom we call a sage, indeed has no need to rely upon learning. Below this level, however, there are varying proportions of clarity and turbidity, fineness and coarseness, and consequently gradations of wise and foolish, worthy and unworthy. Once one's psychophysical stuff is partial, selfish desires for external things easily obscure the mind; without learning, one cannot return to one's original state. What, then, is the Way of learning? It is simply to clarify what is turbid, wash away what is coarse, strive to know, and strive to practice, so as to return to the original state of this moral nature and become like a sage—nothing more.

title: 成化十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
孔子生于東魯雖曰轍環天下卒老于行然其
所得乎天者生而知安而行從容中道而全盡
是性則聖人也當時從遊之士三千其衆畏于
匡微服于宋困厄於陳蔡之間而不去孰非欲
學聖人者何獨曾子之學為善耶夫聖人之道
大而能博諸弟子不能徧觀而盡識也故各隨
其氣質之所近而學焉有學其文學者有學其
政事者有學其言語威儀者固皆非衆人之所
能及然於聖人之道抑為末耳外耳專用心於
===
是而欲歸宿於聖人之域是猶欲適越而北其
轅雖終身由之有不能至者烏得為善學哉曾
子之學則不然惟專用心於內焉內者何本之
心身而已彼見聖人之心知無不至而我之心
方懵然于知於是即事即物而求知是理于心
不如聖人之至不已焉聖人之身行無不當而
我之身方錯然于行於是隨時隨處而求得是
理于身不如聖人之當不止焉觀其自省也為
人謀恐其有不忠與人交恐其有不信受之師

punctuated: 孔子生于東魯，雖曰轍環天下，卒老于行，然其所得乎天者，生而知、安而行，從容中道而全盡是性，則聖人也。當時從遊之士三千其衆，畏于匡，微服于宋，困厄於陳、蔡之間而不去，孰非欲學聖人者？何獨曾子之學為善耶？夫聖人之道，大而能博，諸弟子不能徧觀而盡識也，故各隨其氣質之所近而學焉。有學其文學者，有學其政事者，有學其言語、威儀者，固皆非衆人之所能及，然於聖人之道，抑為末耳、外耳。專用心於是，而欲歸宿於聖人之域，是猶欲適越而北其轅，雖終身由之，有不能至者，烏得為善學哉？曾子之學則不然，惟專用心於內焉。內者何？本之心身而已。彼見聖人之心知無不至，而我之心方懵然于知，於是即事即物，而求知是理于心，不如聖人之至不已焉；聖人之身行無不當，而我之身方錯然于行，於是隨時隨處，而求得是理于身，不如聖人之當不止焉。觀其自省也，為人謀恐其有不忠，與人交恐其有不信，受之師
translation_en: Confucius was born in eastern Lu. Although it is said that his carriage tracks circled the world and he eventually grew old in his travels, what he received from Heaven was such that he knew it from birth, practiced it with ease, effortlessly hit the mean of the Way, and completely fulfilled this nature—thus he was a sage. At that time, the scholars who followed and studied with him numbered three thousand. Even when threatened at Kuang, traveling in disguise through Song, and suffering hardship and distress between Chen and Cai, they did not leave him. Who among them did not wish to learn from the sage? Why, then, was the learning of Master Zeng (Zengzi 曾子) alone considered good? Now, the Way of the sage is great and wide-ranging; the various disciples could not observe it in its entirety or comprehend it completely, so each studied according to what was closest to his own psycho-physical endowment. There were those who studied his cultural refinement and learning, those who studied his statecraft, and those who studied his speech and dignified demeanor. To be sure, none of them could be equaled by ordinary people, yet with respect to the Way of the sage, these were merely its branches and externals. To apply one's mind exclusively to such things while wishing to arrive at last in the realm of the sage is like wishing to go to Yue while pointing one's carriage shafts north: even if one follows that path for a whole lifetime, one will never be able to reach it. How could that be considered good learning? The learning of Master Zeng was not like this; he applied his mind exclusively to what is within. What is meant by "within"? Simply taking the mind and the person as the root. He saw that the sage's mind was all-reaching in its knowledge, whereas his own mind was still muddled in knowing; therefore, in every affair and every object he sought to know this principle in his mind, and until he matched the utmost degree of the sage, he would not cease. He saw that the sage's personal conduct was unfailingly fitting in action, whereas his own person was still disorderly in acting; therefore, at every time and in every place he sought to attain this principle in his person, and until he matched the fittingness of the sage, he would not stop. Look at his self-examination: in planning for others, he feared lest he be unfaithful; in associating with friends, he feared lest he be untrustworthy; in what he received from his teacher…

title: 成化十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
恐其有不熟之已省身之外無他念教人也動
容貌斯遠其暴慢正顏色斯近於信出辭氣斯
遠其鄙倍脩身之外無餘功則專用心於內而
不外也可見矣夫惟其用心也專為力也久如
此是以氣之未清者日以澄而性之本體呈露
質之未美者日以汰而性之大用流行此一貫
之告一唯之對所以不在彼而在此而卒以傳
聖人之道也歟自是而後承其學者有子思焉
明善誠身之要一皆本之於內子思之後有孟
===
子焉知言養氣之功未嘗施之於外萬世之下
使聖人之道一心相傳若合符節而無弊曽子
之功於是為大視彼諸子之學愈遠而愈失其
真有不可同日語者謂之善學也夫奚疑哉雖
然豈特曽子為然若顏子從事博文約禮之誨
而至欲罷不能如有所立卓爾之地亦可謂專
用心於內而善學焉者惜乎天不假年守而未
化故聖人嘆其進而未止也噫聖門學者固云
衆矣而卒傳其道者顏曽之外無聞焉後之欲

…he feared he had not yet mastered inside himself; beyond examining his own person, he had no other thought. And when he taught others—that in moving the countenance one thereby keeps far from violence and heedlessness, that in rectifying the expression one thereby draws near to trustworthiness, and that in uttering words and tones one thereby keeps far from vulgarity and impropriety—beyond cultivating his own person, he had no superfluous effort. That he devoted his mind solely to the internal and not to the external can thus be seen! Now, only because his devotion of mind was so focused and his exertion of effort so sustained was the vital energy (qi) that was not yet pure daily clarified until the original substance of human nature was revealed, and the physical disposition that was not yet fine dailyrefined away until the great function of human nature flowed forth. Is this not why the pronouncement of the "one thread binding all" and the response of a single "yes!" did not fall to those others but fell here to him, so that in the end he transmitted the Way of the Sage?

From this time onward, succeeding to his learning there was Zisi 子思, whose essentials of understanding goodness and making the self sincere were all rooted entirely in the internal; and after Zisi there was Mencius (Mengzi 孟子), whose work of understanding words and nourishing vital energy was never applied to the external. Down through ten thousand generations, causing the Way of the Sage to be transmitted from mind to mind, matching like the halves of a tally without defect—in this the achievement of Master Zeng (Zengzi 曾子) was great indeed. Compared with the learning of those other disciples, which the further it went the more it lost its truth, they cannot be spoken of on the same day. To call him "good at learning"—what doubt can there be?

Even so, how was it only Master Zeng who was thus? Someone like Master Yan (Yanzi 顏子), who pursued the instruction of "broadening oneself with learning and restraining oneself with ritual" until he reached the state where "even if I wished to stop I could not" and where "it seems to stand right before me, towering," may also be called one who devoted his mind solely to the internal and was good at learning. Alas, Heaven did not grant him years, so that he held fast to it without yet being completely transformed by it; therefore the Sage lamented that "I saw him advancing, and never saw him stop." Ah! translation_en:
…Your Imperial Majesty: endowed by Heaven with sage qualities, Your eminent virtue ascends daily. With spiritual receptivity You carry on the grand enterprise of Your Illustrious Ancestors, and with reverent devotion You fulfill great filial piety toward the Palace of Motherly Compassion [the Empress Dowager]. In renewing governance, You have placed foremost importance on men of talent. Holding that for assisting and nourishing the sovereign's virtue nothing surpasses the Classics Colloquium (jingyan), and that for expanding transformative governance one must rely on Confucian learning, You have thereby enabled a lowly scholar from the rustic wilds to behold Your Heavenly Countenance from but a few feet away—stirring the present age and shedding radiance across a thousand antiquities. How could Your servant dare not apply himself with utmost vigor to what he has learned, and further cultivate his own person? Awaiting the mutual sincerity that inspires resolve [alluding to the Hexagram Tai in the Book of Changes], I shall offer counsel to enrich Your mind, hoping to leave something worthy of transmission to posterity and so not fail Your profound grace.

I humbly reflect that the Way of emperors and kings is nowhere more complete than in the Classics, and that the learning of a ruler lies solely in reverence. To set forth the foundational threads of sage learning and the deep subtleties of the Supreme Way is indeed the earnest wish of Your humble servant; to remain ever mindful that "Heaven is manifest, and its Mandate is not easily preserved" [quoting the Book of Odes] is truly the fine rule for an enlightened sovereign. I humbly pray that You take to heart the words of the Book of Changes (Yi), the Book of Documents (Shu), the Book of Odes (Shi), the Record of Rites (Li), and the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu), and embody the virtues of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, King Wen, and King Wu. …while working from before dawn until after dark, always preserve a reverent awe; in meting out punishments and bestowing rewards, and in Your daily conduct and repose, be ever more vigilant against indolence and neglect. Like King Cheng relying on the Duke of Zhou, let none whom You employ be other than upright men; like Gaozong employing Fu Yue, let what is set forth before You take only the ancient precepts as its teacher. 之旨所以必以是為首務也先儒楊氏謂
堯舜所以為萬世法亦率是性而已者其
有見於是歟請因其言而推之是性也具
于人心為五常曰仁義禮智信見諸行事
為五倫曰君臣父子夫婦長幼朋友古之
君臨天下者帝莫聖於堯舜堯曰以親九
族舜曰慎徽五典所以親族徽典者皆是

punctuated: 聖祖神宗垂世立教之典，有宋諸儒著書立言之旨，所以必以是為首務也。先儒楊氏謂「堯、舜所以為萬世法，亦率是性而已」者，其有見於是歟？請因其言而推之。是性也，具于人心為五常，曰仁、義、禮、智、信；見諸行事為五倫，曰君臣、父子、夫婦、長幼、朋友。古之君臨天下者，帝莫聖於堯、舜。堯曰「以親九族」，舜曰「慎徽五典」；所以親族、徽典者，皆是性之見諸行事者也。王莫聖於禹、湯、文、武。禹曰「彝倫攸敘」，湯曰「肇脩人紀」，文、武曰「重民五教」；所以敘倫、脩紀、重教者，亦是性之見諸行事者也。聖有先後，而治無先後之殊；人有古今，而性無古今之異。堯、舜、禹、湯、文、武之為君，既本是性以為治矣；則我朝之列聖，豈能外是性以為化成天下之具哉？欽惟太祖高皇帝以聖神之德，除胡元之亂，慮斯民未復乎是性也，創業垂統之初，即有申明
translation_en:
…the Sacred Ancestor and Divine Progenitor handed down to posterity and established teachings, and why the aim of the various Confucian scholars of the Song dynasty in writing books and establishing doctrines necessarily took this [human nature] as their foremost priority. When the former Confucian Master Yang [Yang Shi 楊時] said, "That whereby Yao and Shun served as models for ten thousand generations was simply that they followed this nature and nothing more," did he not have insight into this? Allow me to build upon his words and extend their meaning.

This nature, as endowed within the human mind, constitutes the Five Constant Virtues: benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and trustworthiness. As manifested in practical conduct, it constitutes the Five Relationships: ruler and minister, father and son, husband and wife, elder and younger, and friend and friend. Among those in antiquity who ruled over All Under Heaven, no emperors were more sagely than Yao and Shun. Concerning Yao it is said, "thereby harmonizing the nine grades of kinsmen," and concerning Shun it is said, "he carefully set forth the beauty of the five cardinal duties." That whereby they harmonized kinsmen and set forth the duties was in every case this nature manifested in practical conduct. No kings were more sagely than Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu. Concerning Yu it is said, "the invariable human relationships were thereby set in order"; concerning Tang it is said, "he began to cultivate the human bonds"; and concerning Wen and Wu it is said, "they attached great importance to the people's five teachings." That whereby they set relationships in order, cultivated the bonds, and emphasized the teachings was likewise this nature manifested in practical conduct.

Sages appeared earlier and later, yet in governance there is no divergence between earlier and later; men have lived in ancient and modern times, yet in human nature there is no difference between ancient and modern. Since Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu, in acting as rulers, already rooted themselves in this nature to govern, how then could the Successive Sages of our Dynasty go outside this nature for the means to transform and perfect All Under Heaven?

Looking up in reverence, the Grand Progenitor, Emperor Gao [the Hongwu Emperor], through his sagely and divine virtue swept away the disorder of the barbarian Yuan. Concerned lest the people had not yet returned to this nature, at the very beginning of founding the enterprise and bequeathing the succession he issued the Edict Clarifying…

text:
五常之誥
太宗文皇帝繼體守成重光恊德既命儒臣纂
集五經四書大全矣慮斯民猶未明乎是
性也復有性理大全之編我
聖祖神宗嘉惠天下後世之意其與堯舜禹湯
文武本是性以垂世立教之意真異世而
同符矣然書之首卷所載太極圖通書濂
溪周子之所作也圖言中正仁義書言五
常百行非是性之根于心而見諸事者乎
===
西銘正蒙橫渠張子之所作也西銘言天
地之帥吾其性正蒙言性者萬物之一原
非是性之出于天而賦于人者乎至於皇
極經世書康節邵子之所作也其言曰命
之在我之謂性性之在物之謂理又非是
性之根于心而見諸事者乎之數子者之
立言固有攸當然究其旨歸其與前代

punctuated: 《五常之誥》。太宗文皇帝繼體守成，重光恊德，既命儒臣纂集《五經四書大全》矣，慮斯民猶未明乎是性也，復有《性理大全》之編。我聖祖、神宗嘉惠天下後世之意，其與堯、舜、禹、湯、文、武本是性以垂世立教之意，真異世而同符矣。然書之首卷所載《太極圖》、《通書》，濂溪周子之所作也。《圖》言中正仁義，《書》言五常百行，非是性之根于心而見諸事者乎？《西銘》、《正蒙》，橫渠張子之所作也。《西銘》言「天地之帥吾其性」，《正蒙》言「性者，萬物之一原」，非是性之出于天而賦于人者乎？至於《皇極經世書》，康節邵子之所作也。其言曰：「命之在我之謂性，性之在物之謂理。」又非是性之根于心而見諸事者乎？之數子者之立言固有攸當，然究其旨歸，其與前代帝王性理之訓、太祖高皇帝《五常之誥》，亦豈不同條而共貫哉？
translation_en: … Announcement Clarifying the Five Constant Virtues (Shenming wuchang zhi gao). Emperor Taizong Wen, succeeding to the throne and preserving the dynasty's achievements, renewed the dynastic brilliance and harmonized his virtue with that of his predecessor. Having already ordered his Confucian officials to compile the Great Compendium of the Five Classics and Four Books (Wujing Sishu daquan), and concerned lest the people still did not understand this human nature, he further commissioned the compilation of the Great Compendium on Nature and Principle (Xingli daquan). The intention of our Sacred Progenitor and Divine Ancestor to bestow blessings upon the empire and future generations truly tallies across different ages with the intention of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu in basing themselves upon this nature to hand down norms to the world and establish teachings. Now, the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate (Taijitu) and Penetrating the Book of Changes (Tongshu) included in the opening scroll of this work were written by Master Zhou of Lianxi (Zhou Dunyi 周敦頤). The Diagram speaks of centrality, correctness, humaneness, and righteousness, while the Book speaks of the Five Constant Virtues and the hundred conducts—is this not human nature rooted in the mind and manifested in affairs? The Western Inscription (Ximing) and Correcting Youthful Ignorance (Zhengmeng) were written by Master Zhang of Hengqu (Zhang Zai 張載). The Western Inscription states, "That which directs Heaven and Earth is my nature," and Correcting Youthful Ignorance states, "Nature is the single source of the myriad things"—is this not human nature issuing from Heaven and endowed in man? As for the Book of Supreme World-Ordering Principles (Huangji jingshi shu), it was written by Master Shao Kangjie (Shao Yong 邵雍). His words say: "The mandate as it resides in me is called nature; nature as it resides in things is called principle"—and is this not once again human nature rooted in the mind and manifested in affairs? The teachings established by these several masters certainly each have their proper validity, yet if we examine their ultimate purport, how could they not share the same threads and be unified by the same governing principle as the instructions on nature and principle of the emperors and kings of former dynasties and the Announcement on the Five Constant Virtues of Emperor Taizu Gao?

聖君之所以為治、諸儒之所以立言，皆不外乎是性如此。而宋儒歐陽脩乃有「聖人教人，性非所先」之言。夫性之於人，與生俱生，不可一日離者也。有天下國家者，外是性以為治，則將棄仁義禮智之常理，而従事於異端邪說矣；舎君臣、父子、夫婦、長幼、朋友之常道，而従事於權謀術數矣。堯、舜、禹、湯、文、武之所以垂世立教，我祖宗列聖之所以化成天下者，固如是哉？愚生佩服聖訓有年矣，性理之說猶未造其閫奥，姑摭所聞如此，執事其進而教之。

第二問
劉繼武
同考試官訓導戴批：首試經書，認理真切，本為以子為最；及觀策場，文辭雄健，滔滔無滯，該博之學、經濟之才、昌大之氣，於是可見。而此篇條對経頼聖賢真儒以明，尤無遺失。秋闈高擢，舎子其誰？
translation_en:
Thus, that by which the sage-rulers governed and that by which the various Confucian scholars established their teachings never went beyond this human nature. Yet the Song scholar Ouyang Xiu 歐陽脩 actually made the statement that "when the sages taught people, human nature was not their first priority." Now, human nature in relation to man is born together with life itself and cannot be parted from for a single day. If those who possess the Empire and the state set aside this human nature in order to govern, they will abandon the constant principles of benevolence, righteousness, ritual propriety, and wisdom, and engage in heterodox and perverse doctrines; they will cast aside the constant ways of ruler and minister, father and son, husband and wife, elder and younger, and friend and friend, and engage in权謀術數 (expedient schemes and manipulative statecraft). Was that by which Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, King Wen, and King Wu handed down teachings to the world, and that by which our Imperial Ancestors and Successive Sage-Emperors transformed and perfected the Empire, really like that? I, a foolish student, have cherished and abided by the Sacred Instructions for years, yet in the doctrines of human nature and principle I have still not reached their inner depths. I tentatively gather what I have heard in this manner; may Your Excellency bring me forward and instruct me.

Second Question
Liu Jiwu 劉繼武
Comment by Associate Examiner Dai, Assistant Instructor (訓導): In the first session on the Five Classics and Four Books, your grasp of principle was genuine and incisive; in my division [本房, misprinted as 本為?], I ranked you the very best. When I came to examine your essays in the policy session, the diction was vigorous and robust, flowing on without obstruction; your broad learning, statecraft talent, and magnificent vital energy can all be seen therein. Moreover, in this essay your point-by-point response clarifies how the Classics rely on the sages, worthies, and true Confucians to be illuminated [経頼聖賢真儒以明], leaving nothing out at all. For high selection in the autumn examination hall, if not you, then who?

title: 成化十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
同考試官教授裘批此策事核而辭豐氣充而
理直末以論孟為六經之本尤條析明白讀之可愛真有學
有識之士也
考試官侍讀周批剖析經疑灼有定見士之
負才積學者也况前塲之作通暢無疵魁選之擢吾
有所歸矣
考試官左庶子劉批經疑一策塲中士子多為
所窘惟此隨問隨答畧無留滯非素有抱負者疇克
爾耶叅之前塲詞理明暢才氣充蔚足知為佳士矣置
===
之首選當合輿論
諸經之傳註經真儒之手而後定諸經之
義理本聖賢之書而後明盖經以載道聖
賢真儒皆是道之所賴以明者也傳註不
經真儒之手固無自而定義理不本聖賢
之書亦何自而明哉請攄所聞以復執事
之間夫易書詩春秋禮記皆聖人載道之
經也自漢以来易也有京房之學有焦延
壽之學書也有伏生之今文有孔氏之古

諸經之傳註經眞儒之手而後定諸經之
義理本聖賢之書而後明蓋經以載道聖
賢眞儒皆是道之所賴以明者也傳註不
經眞儒之手固無自而定義理不本聖賢

壽之學書也有伏生之今文有孔氏之古
punctuated:
同考試官教授裘批：此策事核而辭豐，氣充而理直。末以《論》、《孟》為六經之本，尤條析明白，讀之可愛，真有學有識之士也。
考試官侍讀周批：剖析經疑，灼有定見，士之負才積學者也。况前塲之作，通暢無疵，魁選之擢，吾有所歸矣。
考試官左庶子劉批：經疑一策，塲中士子多為所窘，惟此隨問隨答，畧無留滯，非素有抱負者，疇克爾耶？叅之前塲，詞理明暢，才氣充蔚，足知為佳士矣。置之首選，當合輿論。
諸經之傳註，經真儒之手而後定；諸經之義理，本聖賢之書而後明。盖經以載道，聖賢真儒，皆是道之所賴以明者也。傳註不經真儒之手，固無自而定；義理不本聖賢之書，亦何自而明哉？請攄所聞，以復執事之間。夫《易》、《書》、《詩》、《春秋》、《禮記》，皆聖人載道之經也。自漢以来，《易》也有京房之學，有焦延壽之學；《書》也有伏生之今文，有孔氏之古

Associate Examiner and Instructor (jiaoshou) Qiu comments: In this policy essay, the facts are verified and the diction is rich, the vital force is full and the reasoning is sound. At the end, taking the Analects (Lunyu) and Mencius (Mengzi) as the foundation of the Six Classics, its item-by-item analysis is especially clear and a delight to read. Truly, he is a scholar of both learning and insight.

Examiner and Academician Reader-in-Waiting (shidu) Zhou comments: In analyzing the doubts concerning the Classics, he clearly possesses settled views; he is a scholar endowed with talent and accumulated learning. Moreover, his compositions in the preceding sessions were fluent and flawless. For the selection of the top candidate, I have found where the honor belongs.

Examiner and Left Mentor (zuo shuzi) Liu comments: With this policy question on doubts concerning the Classics, most of the candidates in the examination compound were stymied. Only this essay answers each point as it is asked, without the slightest hesitation or obstruction. Were he not someone who has long cherished high aspirations, who could have achieved this? Comparing it with his work in the preceding sessions, where the expression and reasoning were clear and fluent and the talent and vital force were abundant and luxuriant, it is enough to know that he is an excellent scholar. Placing him first in the selection should accord with public opinion.

The commentaries and annotations on the various Classics were settled only after passing through the hands of true Confucians; the principles and meanings of the various Classics became clear only when grounded in the books of the sages and worthies. For the Classics serve to convey the Way, and the sages, worthies, and true Confucians are all those upon whom this Way relies in order to be made clear. If commentaries and annotations do not pass through the hands of true Confucians, they certainly have no basis on which to be settled; if principles and meanings are not grounded in the books of the sages and worthies, how then could they ever be made clear? Allow me to set forth what I have heard in order to reply to Your Excellency's question [reading 間 as 問].

Now the Book of Changes (Yi), the Book of Documents (Shu), the Book of Odes (Shi), the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu), and the Record of Rites (Liji) are all Classics by which the sages conveyed the Way. Since the Han dynasty, for the Book of Changes there has been the learning of Jing Fang 京房 and the learning of Jiao Yanshou 焦延壽; for the Book of Documents there has been the New Text of Master Fu (Fu Sheng 伏生) and the Old [Text] of the Kong 孔 clan…

title: 成化十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
文詩則有齊魯韓毛之殊其家春秋則有
左氏公穀之異其傳以至禮記亦有大戴
小戴之分其派焉專門名家師異㫖殊而
各為傳註也多矣然見道不明臆說紛起
本以傳經而經反為之鑿本以明經而經
反為之晦迨至有宋隆興真儒輩出痛削
傳註之舛訛丕振斯文之氣脉迂生陋儒
之穿鑿一掃而空之而聖經賢傳如日麗
天如水行地似無可疑者矣執事尚以所
===
疑教諸生愚敢合其異而歸之同焉夫程
子易傳朱子嘗稱其義理精字數足矣雖
以其未及卜筮而復有本義之作然亦足
其所未盡補其所未圓何嘗出於程傳之
外乎蔡氏書傳二典禹謨朱子盖嘗是正
矣其未及是正者亦皆引用師說得之指
授何有於罅隙之可議乎詩傳朱子雖嘗
以為無復遺恨然義理之所得孰如論孟
之多故復有雞肋之喻焉春秋傳程子以

文；《詩》則有齊、魯、韓、毛之殊其家；《春秋》則有左氏、公、穀之異其傳；以至《禮記》亦有大戴、小戴之分其派焉。專門名家，師異㫖殊，而各為傳註也多矣。然見道不明，臆說紛起，本以傳經而經反為之鑿，本以明經而經反為之晦。迨至有宋隆興，真儒輩出，痛削傳註之舛訛，丕振斯文之氣脉，迂生陋儒之穿鑿一掃而空之，而聖經賢傳如日麗天、如水行地，似無可疑者矣。執事尚以所疑教諸生，愚敢合其異而歸之同焉。

夫程子《易傳》，朱子嘗稱其義理精、字數足矣。雖以其未及卜筮而復有《本義》之作，然亦足其所未盡、補其所未圓，何嘗出於《程傳》之外乎？蔡氏《書傳》，《二典》、《禹謨》，朱子盖嘗是正矣；其未及是正者，亦皆引用師說，得之指授，何有於罅隙之可議乎？《詩傳》，朱子雖嘗以為無復遺恨，然義理之所得孰如《論》、《孟》之多？故復有「雞肋」之喻焉。《春秋傳》，程子以
translation_en:
…text; for the Classic of Poetry (Shi), there were the distinct schools of Qi, Lu, Han, and Mao; for the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu), there were the differing traditions of Zuo, Gongyang, and Guliang; and even for the Record of Rites (Liji), there was the division into the branches of the Elder Dai (Da Dai) and Younger Dai (Xiao Dai). Specialized masters of famous schools differed in their teachers and diverged in their interpretations, each producing numerous commentaries and annotations. Yet because their perception of the Way was unclear, conjectural theories sprang up in profusion. Though they originally intended to transmit the Classics, the Classics were instead distorted by them; though they originally intended to elucidate the Classics, the Classics were instead obscured by them. When the Song dynasty rose to prosperity, true Confucians emerged in succession. They thoroughly excised the errors and corruptions of the commentaries and annotations, greatly revitalized the lifeblood of This Culture, and swept away at a single stroke the forced interpretations of pedantic scholars and narrow-minded Confucians. Thus the Classics of the sages and the commentaries of the worthies became like the sun shining in the heavens and water coursing over the earth, leaving seemingly nothing to be doubted. Since Your Reverence still instructs the candidates with these doubts, I venture to reconcile their differences and bring them back to unity.

As for Master Cheng's [Cheng Yi 程頤] Commentary on the Changes (Yi zhuan), Master Zhu [Zhu Xi 朱熹] once praised its moral principles as refined and its wording as sufficient. Although he subsequently composed the Original Meaning (Benyi) because Cheng's work had not addressed divination by tortoise-shell and milfoil, this merely supplied what it had not fully exhausted and rounded out what it had left incomplete—how could it ever have gone beyond the bounds of the Cheng Commentary? As for Mr. Cai's [Cai Shen 蔡沈] Commentary on the Documents (Shu zhuan), Master Zhu had in fact corrected the sections on the "Two Canons" ("Er dian") and the "Counsels of Yu" ("Yu mo"); and as for the parts he did not live to correct, they too all cited his master's doctrines and were obtained from his personal instruction—how could there be any flaws or gaps open to criticism? As for the Commentary on the Poetry (Shi zhuan), although Master Zhu once considered it to leave no further regrets, how could what one gains in moral principles from the Poetry compare in abundance to that from the Analects (Lunyu) and Mencius (Mengzi)? Hence he also made the analogy of "chicken ribs" (jile, something of slight value yet hard to discard). Such notions as taking a single word as praise or blame, or the recording of days and months as a moral convention, may perhaps not have been the intention of the Sage, which is why Master Zhu [Zhu Xi 朱熹] made the criticism that its moral principles were forced and far-fetched. As for the Record of Rites (Liji), although it is said to have come variously from the hands of Han-dynasty scholars, among its contents are maxims and supreme discourses that no Han scholar could have attained; those who consider it merely the doctrines of Han scholars are mistaken. Although Master Chen's [Chen Hao 陳澔] Collected Explanations (Jishuo) occasionally employs his own views, in its broad outlines and main thrust it mostly corroborates them with the words of eminent scholars, and never fails to capture the intentions of those who recorded the rites. Spoken of from this perspective, what doubt can there be regarding the commentaries and annotations of the Song-dynasty scholars! Even so, the Six Classics are all wherein the wondrous Way and subtle meanings of the sages reside; there are indeed scholars who exhaust them until their heads turn white without being able to glimpse their inner recesses, yet if one seeks their essentials, there is a foundation. Therefore Master Cheng said: "Scholars ought to take the Analects (Lunyu) and the Mencius (Mengzi) as the foundation. Once the Analects and the Mencius are mastered, the Six Classics can become clear even without being specifically studied." For the principles of the Six Classics are gathered in the Analects and the Mencius, and the principles of the Analects and the Mencius thread through the Six Classics; once the Analects and the Mencius are mastered, the foundation is rectified, and when one uses them to study the Six Classics, one is already more than halfway to understanding. title: 成化十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
人也以法為之先耳此漢唐宋所以不古
若也然則考課之法必德法並任斯為美
乎請以是為明問復夫天生兆民不能自
治而必樹之君君主兆民不能獨理而必
付之臣使天下之臣各稱其任則天下自
治雖不俟於考課可也奈何位公卿者不
皆賢也列庶職者不皆善也便佞倖進之
門闢而疏遠方正之途塞官冗政貪吏恣
民弊勢所必至考課之法奚容以不立哉
===
是故唐虞成周亦必恃此以為治三載考
績三考黜陟幽明唐虞考課之大綱也盖
其居位久而受任專立法寬而責效遠故
鯀之罪不在方命圯族之日而在九載弗
績之時禹之賞不在九河既道之際而在
九州攸同之後豈云簡哉三歲計吏治九
年大明黜陟成周考課之大綱也盖其自
下考其属而總之於太宰太宰第其功過
而後詔王廢置故日成月要歲會正以見

punctuated:
人也，以法為之先耳，此漢、唐、宋所以不古若也。然則考課之法，必德、法並任，斯為美乎？請以是為明問復。

夫天生兆民，不能自治，而必樹之君；君主兆民，不能獨理，而必付之臣。使天下之臣各稱其任，則天下自治，雖不俟於考課可也。奈何位公卿者不皆賢也，列庶職者不皆善也，便佞倖進之門闢，而疏遠方正之途塞，官冗政貪，吏恣民弊，勢所必至，考課之法奚容以不立哉？是故唐、虞、成周亦必恃此以為治。「三載考績，三考黜陟幽明」，唐、虞考課之大綱也。盖其居位久而受任專，立法寬而責效遠，故鯀之罪不在「方命圯族」之日，而在「九載弗績」之時；禹之賞不在「九河既道」之際，而在「九州攸同」之後，豈云簡哉？「三歲計吏治，九年大明黜陟」，成周考課之大綱也。盖其自下考其属而總之於太宰，太宰第其功過而後詔王廢置，故日成、月要、歲會，正以見
translation_en:
…capable men; it is simply that they put law first. This is why the Han, Tang, and Song failed to match antiquity. This being so, must the system of personnel evaluation employ both virtue and law together in order to be admirable? Allow me to offer this in reply to Your Brilliant Inquiry.

Now, when Heaven brings forth the multitude of people, they cannot govern themselves, so a ruler must be established for them; when a ruler presides over the multitude of people, he cannot manage them alone, so he must entrust the task to his officials. If the officials of the realm each proved equal to their responsibilities, the realm would be well governed of itself, and one would not even need to rely on personnel evaluations. Yet how is it that those occupying the positions of dukes and ministers are not all worthy, and those arrayed in the various offices are not all good? When the gates for sycophants and opportunists to advance are thrown open, while the paths for the upright and candid are blocked and they are kept at a distance, superfluous officials and greedy administration, unrestrained subofficial functionaries and an exhausted populace are the inevitable result. How, then, could a system of personnel evaluation not be established?

For this reason, even Tang, Yu, and the Flourishing Zhou had to rely on this to achieve good governance. "Every three years there was an examination of achievements, and after three examinations the undeserving were demoted and the deserving promoted"—this was the grand outline of personnel evaluation in Tang and Yu. Indeed, because officials held their posts for a long time and received專 [exclusive/undivided] mandates, while the laws established were lenient and the results demanded were long-term, Gun's punishment did not occur on the day he "disobeyed orders and ruined his clan," but at the time when "for nine years his work was unaccomplished"; and Yu's reward did not take place at the moment when "the Nine Rivers were conducted to their proper channels," but only after "the Nine Provinces were made uniform." How could this be called overly simple? "Every three years to audit the governance of officials, and after nine years to make a grand clarification of demotions and promotions"—this was the grand outline of personnel evaluation in the Flourishing Zhou. Indeed, each superior evaluated his own subordinates from the bottom up, and the results were aggregated under the Grand Councilor (Taizai); the Grand Councilor graded their merits and faults and only then advised the King on their dismissal or placement. Thus, the daily tallies, monthly summaries, and annual accounts served precisely to reveal…

text:
其功過之漸小宰之六計宰夫之八職正
以析其善惡之詳豈云煩哉故夫庶政惟
和而萬邦咸寧推賢讓能而萬邦無斁所
謂純於任德者如此豈後世所可及哉繼
周之後曰漢考課之行於當時則郡守得
課令長刺史得課守相丞相考其計天子
受其要周之意猶在也觀夫蕭曹開基于
前丙魏有聲於後則其所得之人也黎民
醇厚天下富庶則其致治之效也繼漢之
===

有三恪七事之評比漢固為密視古則相
遠矣而其得人之效則房杜姚宋也韓范

慶曆之君子滿朝也然暫得而即失暫盛
而即衰所謂純於任法者如此豈能比隆
於前古哉至若京房陳任法之說劉邵功

translation_en:
… the gradual accumulation of their merits and faults; while the Six Audits (liuji) of the Junior Ministro (Xiaozai) and the Eight Duties (bazhi) of the Chief Steward (Zaifu) were precisely to analyze the details of their good and evil deeds—how could this be called overly complicated? Therefore, all affairs of state were harmonious and the myriad states were all at peace; the worthy were promoted and the able yielded to, and the myriad states never grew weary. Such was what has been called relying purely on virtue—how could later ages ever match it?

Succeeding the Zhou was the Han. In the practice of personnel evaluation at that time, Commandery Governors (Junshou) were empowered to evaluate District Magistrates and Chiefs (Lingzhang), Regional Inspectors (Cishi) were empowered to evaluate Commandery Governors and Princely State Chancellors (Shouxiang), the Counselor-in-Chief (Chengxiang) examined their accounts, and the Son of Heaven received their summaries; the spirit of the Zhou still remained. Looking at how Xiao He 蕭何 and Cao Shen 曹參 laid the foundations in the early period, and how Bing Ji 丙吉 and Wei Xiang 魏相 won renown later on, those were the men it obtained; that the common people were simple and honest and the empire was wealthy and populous, those were the results of its achievement of good governance.

Succeeding the Han were the Tang and the Song. The Tang had the evaluation of the Four Virtues (sishan) and Twenty-seven Qualifications (ershiqi zui), while the Song had the assessment of the Three Diligences (sanke) and Seven Matters (qishi). Compared to the Han, these were certainly more detailed, yet compared to antiquity, they were far removed. As for the results of their obtaining men of talent, there were Fang Xuanling 房玄齡, Du Ruhui 杜如晦, Yao Chong 姚崇, and Song Jing 宋璟 in the Tang, and Han Qi 韓琦, Fan Zhongyan 范仲淹, Fu Bi 富弼, and Ouyang Xiu 歐陽修 in the Song; as for the flourishing of their achievement of governance, there was the price of a peck of rice at ten cash during the Zhenguan reign (627–649), and the court filled with gentlemen during the Qingli reign (1041–1048). Yet what was briefly gained was soon lost, and what briefly flourished soon declined. Such was what has been called relying purely on laws—how could it rival the splendor of high antiquity?

As for Jing Fang 京房 presenting his theory of relying on laws, and Liu Shao 劉邵 proposing that Commandery Governors be appointed by order of merit—these seemed appropriate, yet erred in being overly complicated. And as for Cui Lin 崔林 submitting his discourse on relying on men, and Du Yu 杜預 determining retention or dismissal by general superiority or inferiority—these seemed judicious, yet erred in being …

punctuated: 太簡。其在當時且不能行，而可行之於今乎？洪惟我朝稽古建官，法制精密，盖與唐、虞、成周異世同符，行之萬代而無弊者也。然而是非好惡或不能盡出於公，黜陟予奪或不能舉得其當，此豈法之過哉？奉行者之未至耳。故聖天子為天下慮，重下考察之詔，天下之吏宜知有所勸懲矣。而執事又以下詢承學，不揣狂妄，以德、法兼任為獻。誠使今日司考課者，惟成憲之是遵，惟聖意之是體，必公以存心而權勢所不屈，明以照物而清濁之不淆。果賢耶，從而陟之；果不賢耶，從而黜之。由是奔競者無所容，恬退者日以進，公卿于以得人，庶職于以稱任。士風之淳，治化之美，唐、虞、成周豈得專其美於前哉！謹對。
translation_en:
… being overly simplistic. If these could not even be practiced in their own time, how could they be practiced today?

Reflecting upon our Great Dynasty, it examined antiquity to establish offices, and its laws and institutions are precise and thorough. Indeed, though in a different era from Tang, Yu, and Flourishing Zhou, it matches them like the two halves of a tally, and its system can be practiced for ten thousand generations without abuse. Yet at times judgments of right and wrong, or likes and dislikes, cannot all stem from impartiality, and demotions and promotions, or rewards and deprivations, cannot all be entirely appropriate. How could this be the fault of the laws? It is simply that those who administer them have fallen short.

Therefore, the Sacred Son of Heaven, taking thought for the empire, has repeatedly issued edicts on personnel evaluation, so the officials of the empire ought to know how to be encouraged and warned. Now Your Excellency again inquiries of us junior scholars below; without measuring my own rashness and presumption, I offer the view that virtue and law should be relied upon together. If indeed those in charge of personnel evaluation today would only abide by the established statutes and embody the sacred intentions—unfailingly preserving impartiality in their minds so as not to bend before power and influence, and illuminating affairs with clarity so that the pure and the turbid are not confused; if someone is truly worthy, accordingly promoting him, and if someone is truly unworthy, accordingly demoting him—then ambitious self-seekers will have nowhere to be tolerated, while the modest and retiring will advance day by day; the high ministers will thereby obtain the right men, and the myriad offices will thereby be filled by those equal to their duties. With the purity of scholarly ethos and the beauty of transformative governance, how could Tang, Yu, and Flourishing Zhou monopolize such glory in the past! I respectfully reply.

text:
第四問
同考試官訓導戴批人才偏全由於學術正否
而治道隆替所攸繫此篇條答詳明辭氣整密其策中
之傑然者
同考試官教授褒批人才一策敷答詳明才思沛

術正否有講貫者也真才之學尚其勉之
===
考試官左庶子劉批論正學真才語意分明殆
嘗留心於是者
欲致天下之治當求乎真才欲求人才之
真當考乎學術盖學術者人才之本而人
才者致治之原也學術正則人才真真才
出則天下治此執事發策秋闈所以拳拳
於真才之訪也夫人之才雖禀于天而才
之成亦由于學學之正否人才之真不真
繫焉古之有天下國家者養育人才盖有

Fourth Question

Associate Examiner and Assistant Instructor (xundao) Dai comments: "Whether human talent is partial or complete depends on whether scholarly learning is orthodox or not, and upon this hinges the flourishing or decline of the Way of governance. This essay answers point by point with clarity and detail, and its phrasing and tone are orderly and tight; it is an outstanding piece among the policy essays."
Associate Examiner and Instructor (jiaoshou) Bao [?] comments: "In this policy essay on human talent, the exposition and answers are detailed and clear, and the talent and thought flow abundantly. In the end, he holds himself to the standard of the sages and worthies; he may truly be called a scholar of high aspiration."
Examiner and Academician Reader-in-Waiting (shidu) Zhou comments: "Discussing whether the scholarly learning of the ancients was orthodox or not on the basis of their words, deeds, and Way of governance shows that he has thoroughly studied these matters. May he continue to strive in the learning that produces true talent."
Examiner and Left Mentor of the Household Administration of the Heir Apparent (zuo shuzi) Liu comments: "In discussing orthodox learning and true talent, the expression and meaning are clear and distinct; he is no doubt someone who has paid close attention to these matters."

If one wishes to bring about the governance of the Empire, one must seek true talent; if one wishes to seek what is true in human talent, one must examine scholarly learning. For scholarly learning is the root of human talent, and human talent is the source of bringing about governance. When scholarly learning is orthodox, human talent is true; when true talent emerges, the Empire is well governed. This is why Your Excellency, in propounding the policy questions in the autumn examination compound, has been so earnestly concerned with inquiring after true talent. Now, although a person's talent is endowed by Heaven, the completion of that talent also comes from learning; whether learning is orthodox or not determines whether human talent is true or not. Those in antiquity who possessed the Empire and the state, in nurturing human talent, indeed had…

title: 成化十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
道矣是故始之以格物致知使求知是理
于心繼之以誠意正心脩身使求行是理
于身終之以齊家治國平天下使推行是
理于人其序之不可亂功之不可缺也如
此是以當時聖賢之真才胥此焉出而雍
熈泰和之善治胥此焉成也苟或不此之
務而從事于記誦焉為口耳之贅文辭焉
為枝葉之末則其學也愈博愈工而愈去
聖賢之道遠矣若是而望其真才之成烏
===
可得哉古之真才見用於世者在唐虞三
代若臯陶伊傅周召以其言行之存者考
之臯陶有慎厥身脩之謨伊尹有脩身允
德之訓傅說有惟學遜志之言以至周公
之所其無逸召公之王敬作所其言行之
正如此則其學問之正也從可知矣世道
既降才不古若隨世以就功名之士在漢
若蕭何曹參丙吉魏相在唐若房玄齡杜
如晦姚崇宋璟在宋若韓琦范仲淹富弼

punctuated: 道矣。是故始之以格物、致知，使求知是理于心；繼之以誠意、正心、脩身，使求行是理于身；終之以齊家、治國、平天下，使推行是理于人。其序之不可亂、功之不可缺也如此，是以當時聖賢之真才胥此焉出，而雍熈泰和之善治胥此焉成也。苟或不此之務，而從事于記誦焉為口耳之贅，文辭焉為枝葉之末，則其學也，愈博愈工，而愈去聖賢之道遠矣。若是而望其真才之成，烏可得哉？古之真才見用於世者，在唐、虞、三代，若臯陶、伊、傅、周、召，以其言行之存者考之：臯陶有「慎厥身脩」之謨，伊尹有「脩身允德」之訓，傅說有「惟學遜志」之言，以至周公之「所其無逸」、召公之「王敬作所」。其言行之正如此，則其學問之正也從可知矣。世道既降，才不古若。隨世以就功名之士，在漢若蕭何、曹參、丙吉、魏相，在唐若房玄齡、杜如晦、姚崇、宋璟，在宋若韓琦、范仲淹、富弼、
translation_en:
… had a proper Way. Therefore, they began with investigating things and extending knowledge, causing men to seek to know this principle in their minds; they continued with making the intentions sincere, rectifying the mind, and cultivating the person, causing men to seek to practice this principle in their persons; and they concluded with regulating the family, rightly governing the state, and bringing peace to all under Heaven, causing men to extend and practice this principle among others. Such was the order that could not be confused and the effort that could not be omitted. Thus, the true talent of the sages and worthies of that time all emerged from this, and the good governance of harmonious prosperity and supreme peace was all accomplished through this. If, however, one does not devote oneself to this, and instead engages in rote memorization as superfluous talk between mouth and ear, or in literary composition as the trivialities of branches and leaves, then the broader and more skillful one's learning becomes, the further it departs from the Way of the sages and worthies. Doing thus and yet hoping for the perfection of true talent—how could it be attained?

As for the true talents of antiquity who were employed in the world: in the times of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties, there were men such as Gao Yao 臯陶, Yi Yin 伊尹, Fu Yue 傅說, the Duke of Zhou 周公, and the Duke of Shao 召公. If we examine their surviving words and deeds: Gao Yao offered the counsel of "carefully cultivating his person"; Yi Yin gave the instruction of "cultivating the person and being sincere in virtue"; Fu Yue spoke the words of "in learning, having a humble will"; and so on down to the Duke of Zhou's "making 'without-idleness' his dwelling place" and the Duke of Shao's "may the King make reverence his dwelling place." Since their words and deeds were as upright as this, the orthodoxy of their learning can accordingly be known.

Once the Way of the world declined, talent no longer matched antiquity. Among scholars who adapted to their times to achieve merit and fame, in the Han there were men such as Xiao He 蕭何, Cao Can 曹參, Bing Ji 丙吉, and Wei Xiang 魏相; in the Tang, men such as Fang Xuanling 房玄齡, Du Ruhui 杜如晦, Yao Chong 姚崇, and Song Jing 宋璟; and in the Song, men such as Han Qi 韓琦, Fan Zhongyan 范仲淹, Fu Bi 富弼, …

title: 成化十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
歐陽脩以其事功之成者觀之漢之治雜
於伯唐之治雜於夷宋之治雖差盛於漢
唐而不能比隆前古事功之未正如此則
其學問之非正也槩可見矣孔孟既沒正
學寥寥千載之下至宋而始續若濂溪周
子河南两程子横渠張子考亭朱子乃其
尤著者學問之正人才之真無愧于皐陶
伊傅周召矣而不得見用於世徒見于著
書立言講明斯道而已然使其得用則唐
===
虞三代之治将復見於後世宋之治豈直
止於宋而已哉元儒魯齋許氏謂傳記中
人才傑然可觀以道理觀之只是偏才聖
人則圓融渾全百理皆具者蓋以蕭曹丙
魏之流其才固傑然可觀特血氣用事一
偏之才耳而皐陶伊傅周召諸君子則德
性用事故圓融渾全百理皆具蓋即所謂
真才也夫希聖希賢吾儒分内事耳苟能
於此奮然從事于聖賢之正學則何聖賢

translation_en:
… and Ouyang Xiu 歐陽脩—judging by the achievements they brought to fruition, the governance of the Han was mixed with the way of the hegemon, the governance of the Tang was mixed with barbarian ways, and although the governance of the Song was somewhat more flourishing than that of the Han and Tang, it still could not rival the splendor of high antiquity. Since their achievements were less than orthodox to this degree, it can generally be seen that their learning was not orthodox either.

After Confucius and Mencius passed away, orthodox learning fell silent for a thousand years until the Song dynasty, when the transmission was first resumed. Master Zhou of Lianxi (Zhou Dunyi 周敦頤), the two Masters Cheng of Henan (Cheng Hao 程顥 and Cheng Yi 程頤), Master Zhang of Hengqu (Zhang Zai 張載), and Master Zhu of Kaoting (Zhu Xi 朱熹) were the most illustrious among them. In the orthodoxy of their learning and the genuineness of their talent, they had nothing to be ashamed of before Gao Yao 皐陶, Yi Yin 伊尹, Fu Yue 傅說, the Duke of Zhou 周公, and the Duke of Shao 召公. Yet they were unable to be employed in the world and were seen merely writing books, establishing teachings, and elucidating this Way. Had they been employed, however, the governance of Tang (Yao), Yu (Shun), and the Three Dynasties would have been seen again in later ages—how could the governance of the Song have merely stopped at being that of the Song!

The Yuan Confucian scholar Master Xu of Luzhai (Xu Heng 許衡) said: "The men of talent in the historical records are outstanding and impressive to behold, yet when viewed in terms of moral principle, they are merely men of partial talent; the sages, by contrast, are harmoniously integrated and wholly complete, possessing all principles in full." This is because men of the ilk of Xiao He 蕭何, Cao Can 曹參, Bing Ji 丙吉, and Wei Xiang 魏相 certainly had talents that were outstanding and impressive to behold, yet they acted merely from physical vigor and temperament, making theirs a one-sided talent. Noble men such as Gao Yao, Yi Yin, Fu Yue, the Duke of Zhou, and the Duke of Shao, on the other hand, acted from their moral nature; therefore they were harmoniously integrated and wholly complete, possessing all principles in full—which is precisely what is meant by genuine talent.

To aspire to be a sage and to aspire to be a worthy is simply the proper duty of us Confucians. If in this we can rouse ourselves to pursue the orthodox learning of the sages and worthies, then how could the sages' and worthies' …

translation_en:
… true talent of the sages and worthies could not be attained! Stupid as I am, I grew up in the capital region and have been nourished by the sacred transforming influence for years. Although I have certainly not yet been able to peer into the inner depths of the orthodox learning of the sages and worthies, as for the trivial practices of rote memorization and literary phrasing, I would not dare devote myself to them either, lest I betray the profound grace of the court's nurturing. I respectfully offer this in reply to your discerning question.

Fifth Question
Liu Jiwu 劉繼武
Associate Examiner Assistant Instructor Dai 戴 comments: A policy question on current affairs serves precisely to observe a candidate's talent and insight. This essay weighs antiquity and takes the present as its standard, answering point by point appropriately; he is truly a scholar of talent and insight. When he enters service in the future, it is still hoped that he will pour forth his loyalty to repay the state, and not merely consign it to empty words and thereby betray his aspirations.
Associate Examiner Instructor Bao 褒 comments: In answering the policy question on current affairs, his arguments and plans are all well-grounded and practicable. At the end, he traces everything back to the single mind of the ruler of men, which is an argument that gets to the very root of the matter—most commendable, most commendable.
Examiner Academician Reader-in-Waiting Zhou 周 comments: His point-by-point reply to the policy question on current affairs is clear and fluent, and is moreover sufficient to show his talent for practical service, not merely the beauty of his literary grace.
Examiner Left Mentor Liu 劉 comments: All five policy essays in this examination paper are excellent, and those on classical doubts and current affairs in particular surpass all expectations; therefore, we have specially selected this one for publication.

text:
當無虞之日而陳儆戒之謨當有道之世
而思保邦之策此治不忘亂安不忘危唐
虞成周明君賢相之所用心也恭惟
聖天子至仁大德如堯如舜漢文雖賢固不足
以擬之矣而世道熙洽天下治安亦豈有
事之容議哉執事奉
明詔秉文衡而以時務詢諸生且欲生効賈
誼獻忠報國之心而不嫌於流涕太息之
說生有以窺見執事忠愛之心矣顧生無
===

匪其人則受連坐之罰夫如是則賢愚何

矣然資格一拘則賢愚不能不混進保薦
一舉則名實容或有未符昔人嘗欲革之
愚以爲資格所以待常流不必革也惟如
古選官惟賢陟之不嫌於越級涖事惟能
用之不避乎驟進保薦所以獎恬退不必
廢也惟如古舉能其官則有薦賢之賞稱
匪其人則受連坐之罰夫如是則賢愚何
punctuated:
當無虞之日而陳儆戒之謨，當有道之世而思保邦之策，此治不忘亂、安不忘危，唐、虞、成周明君賢相之所用心也。恭惟聖天子至仁大德，如堯如舜，漢文雖賢，固不足以擬之矣。而世道熙洽，天下治安，亦豈有事之容議哉？執事奉明詔，秉文衡，而以時務詢諸生，且欲生効賈誼獻忠報國之心，而不嫌於流涕太息之說，生有以窺見執事忠愛之心矣。顧生無誼才，何以應明問？雖然，不敢負也。

夫理國在人才，掄才在銓選，今之銓選固有定法矣。然資格一拘，則賢愚不能不混進；保薦一舉，則名實容或有未符，昔人嘗欲革之。愚以為資格所以待常流，不必革也，惟如古「建官惟賢」，陟之不嫌於越級；「涖事惟能」，用之不避乎驟進。保薦所以獎恬退，不必廢也，惟如古舉能其官，則有薦賢之賞；稱匪其人，則受連坐之罰。夫如是，則賢愚何⋯⋯
translation_en:
To set forth counsels of caution and admonition in days free from anxiety, and to ponder policies for preserving the state in an age when the Way prevails—this is not forgetting disorder in times of order and not forgetting danger in times of peace, which is that to which the enlightened rulers and worthy ministers of Tang, Yu, and Accomplished Zhou applied their minds. Reverently I reflect that the Sagely Son of Heaven possesses supreme benevolence and great virtue, like Yao and like Shun; although Emperor Wen of Han was worthy, he truly is not sufficient to be compared to Him. Moreover, with the moral state of the world harmonious and prosperous, and All-under-Heaven well-governed and at peace, how could there be any affairs that admit of criticism? You, sir, have received the luminous edict and hold the balance of civil examination, inquiring of this student regarding current affairs; furthermore, you wish for this student to emulate Jia Yi's贾谊 heart of offering loyalty and repaying the state, without taking offense at talk of weeping and sighing deeply—from this I have been able to catch a glimpse of your loyal and affectionate heart, sir! Yet I lack the talent of Jia Yi; how can I respond to your sagacious question? Even so, I dare not fail your expectations.

Now, ordering the state lies in men of talent, and selecting talent lies in personnel evaluation and appointment; today's personnel selection certainly has established laws. Yet once seniority qualifications are rigidly adhered to, the worthy and the foolish cannot avoid advancing together indiscriminately; and once guaranteed recommendation is practiced, reputation and reality may at times fail to correspond. Men of the past once wished to abolish them. In my humble opinion, seniority qualifications are the means to treat ordinary men and need not be abolished: only, as in antiquity when "establishing offices only for the worthy," in promoting them one should not shy away from skipping grades; and when "putting only the capable in charge of affairs," in employing them one should not avoid rapid advancement. Guaranteed recommendation is the means to encourage those who are unassuming and retiring and need not be discarded: only, as in antiquity, if the one recommended is capable in his office, there should be the reward for recommending the worthy; and if one praises an unsuitable person, one should receive the punishment of joint liability. If it is done like this, how would the worthy and the foolish…

title: 成化十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
至於混進而名實何至於未符哉足國在
財賦理財在會計今之會計固有常制矣
然借撥預征之頻加糶穀賣絲之迫切民
力巳竭調發恒闕昔人盖嘗傷之愚以為
借撥非法也預征弊政也皆不可用也惟
驅游手之民以服田罷不及之務以省費
其轉運也必稽簿書之實使奸盜不至於
侵漁出入也必量其盈朒之數使用度不
至於無節夫如是則征輸何患於困竭而
===
調發何患於不足哉將出於膏粱兵歸於
私役誠非威虜之術也苟嚴武舉之選將
惟才謀是用雖膏粱行伍也亦在所必取
申政令之重兵惟訓練之歸雖權門勢家
也亦在所不容則邊防不備非所慮矣政
分於多門刑失於不中誠非輔治之道也
苟循定制而專人以司法使有罪者必致
之刑官體欽恤而罪人必以律使無辜者
不至於濫及則刑罰不中也非所憂矣敎

punctuated: 至於混進，而名實何至於未符哉？足國在財賦，理財在會計。今之會計固有常制矣，然借撥、預征之頻加，糶穀、賣絲之迫切，民力巳竭，調發恒闕，昔人盖嘗傷之。愚以為借撥非法也，預征弊政也，皆不可用也。惟驅游手之民以服田，罷不及之務以省費；其轉運也，必稽簿書之實，使奸盜不至於侵漁；出入也，必量其盈朒之數，使用度不至於無節。夫如是，則征輸何患於困竭，而調發何患於不足哉？將出於膏粱，兵歸於私役，誠非威虜之術也。苟嚴武舉之選，將惟才謀是用，雖膏粱、行伍也，亦在所必取；申政令之重，兵惟訓練之歸，雖權門勢家也，亦在所不容，則邊防不備非所慮矣。政分於多門，刑失於不中，誠非輔治之道也。苟循定制而專人以司法，使有罪者必致之刑官；體欽恤而罪人必以律，使無辜者不至於濫及，則刑罰不中也非所憂矣。敎
translation_en:
… come to advance indiscriminately, and how would reputation and reality fail to correspond?

Enriching the state lies in fiscal revenues, and managing finances lies in accounting. Today's accounting certainly has regular statutes; yet when diversions of funds and advance collections are repeatedly imposed, and when forced sales of new grain and raw silk become pressing, the people's strength is exhausted and allocations for requisitions are constantly short—men of the past indeed lamented this. I humbly consider that diverting funds is unlawful and collecting taxes in advance is a corrupt policy; neither should be used. Only if we drive idle people back to working the fields and halt non-urgent undertakings to save expenses; if, in transport and shipping, we strictly audit the reality of the account books so that crooked thieves cannot embezzle; and if, in revenues and expenditures, we measure the amounts of surplus and deficit so that spending does not become unrestrained—then if it is like this, why worry that tax payments will be exhausted, and why worry that allocations will be insufficient?

When generals come from pampered aristocratic families and soldiers are diverted into private labor service, this is truly no way to overawe the northern tribes. If we make the selection in the military examinations strict so that generals are employed solely on the basis of talent and strategy—taking them without fail whether they come from aristocratic families or the common ranks; and if we reiterate the gravity of government ordinances so that soldiers are devoted solely to training—tolerating no infractions even from powerful and influential families—then unpreparedness in frontier defense will be nothing to worry about.

When administration is divided among many agencies and punishments fail to hit the mark, this is truly not the way to assist governance. If we follow established statutes and assign specialized officials to administer the law, ensuring that offenders are always handed over to judicial officials; and if we embody imperial compassion and always sentence offenders according to the statutory code, ensuring that the innocent are not unjustly implicated—then punishments failing to hit the mark will also be nothing to worry about.

title: 成化十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
化不明而異端起理固然也必脩學校之
制以隆仁義之道使民知所以教則誣世
之燄能不滅乎禮讓不興而姦軌橫勢固
然也必詳鄉飲之制以盡禮讓之節使民
知所以養則訐上之風能不息乎至若乞
墦拜塵士風之汚甚矣此在重清節焉誠
使清節之士處於顯位而諛佞之徒屏之
遠方則士風不期厚而自厚矣帝服后飾
民俗之僭極矣此在謹好尚焉誠使君子
===
皆崇節儉之德小人申以違犯之禁則民
俗不期美而自美矣然嘗聞之表正則影
隨風行則草偃綱紀天下之治固在乎得
賢而取賢之道則本乎君人者之一心耳
君心一正則賢才效職法度脩明而天下
無不正矣所謂正心以正朝廷正朝廷以
正百官正百官以正萬民此之謂也唐虞
三代之盛其要亦不過此變通張弛如斯
而已矣執事倘有取焉還

punctuated: 化不明而異端起，理固然也。必脩學校之制，以隆仁義之道，使民知所以教，則誣世之燄能不滅乎？禮讓不興而姦軌橫，勢固然也。必詳鄉飲之制，以盡禮讓之節，使民知所以養，則訐上之風能不息乎？至若乞墦拜塵，士風之汚甚矣，此在重清節焉。誠使清節之士處於顯位，而諛佞之徒屏之遠方，則士風不期厚而自厚矣。帝服后飾，民俗之僭極矣，此在謹好尚焉。誠使君子皆崇節儉之德，小人申以違犯之禁，則民俗不期美而自美矣。然嘗聞之：表正則影隨，風行則草偃。綱紀天下之治，固在乎得賢，而取賢之道，則本乎君人者之一心耳。君心一正，則賢才效職，法度脩明，而天下無不正矣。所謂「正心以正朝廷，正朝廷以正百官，正百官以正萬民」，此之謂也。唐、虞、三代之盛，其要亦不過此，變通張弛，如斯而已矣。執事倘有取焉，還
translation_en:
…instruction is not made clear, heterodox doctrines arise; this is naturally so in principle. If we without fail cultivate the institution of schools to exalt the way of benevolence and righteousness, causing the people to understand that by which they are taught, then how could the flames that deceive the world not be extinguished? When ritual deference does not flourish, villainy and lawlessness run rampant; this is naturally so by circumstance. If we without fail elaborate the institution of the Community Wine-Drinking Ceremony (xiangyin) to fulfill theobservances of ritual deference, causing the people to understand that by which they are nurtured, then how could the custom of denouncing superiors not cease?

As for begging among the tombs and bowing to the dust of carriages, the debasement of literati ethos has reached an extreme; addressing this lies in valuing pure integrity. Truly, if men of pure integrity are placed in prominent positions while sycophants and flatterers are banished to distant regions, then the literati ethos will become generous of its own accord without our even expecting it. When people wear imperial robes and empresses' ornaments, the presumptuousness of popular customs has reached its limit; addressing this lies in being circumspect about what is favored and esteemed. Truly, if gentlemen all revere the virtue of frugality and the petty are warned with prohibitions against transgression, then popular customs will become admirable of their own accord without our even expecting it.

Yet I have heard it said: when the gnomon is straight, the shadow follows; when the wind blows, the grass bends. Maintaining order in the governance of the realm certainly depends on obtaining worthy men, while the way of selecting worthy men is rooted in the single mind of the ruler of men. Once the ruler's mind is rectified, worthy talents will fulfill their duties, laws and institutions will be cultivated and made clear, and there will be nothing in the realm that is not rectified. The saying, "Rectify the mind in order to rectify the court; rectify the court in order to rectify the hundred officials; rectify the hundred officials in order to rectify the myriad people," refers to this. The flourishing of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties in its essentials went no further than this; adapting to change and alternating tension with relaxation are just like this and nothing more. Should Your Reverences find something worth selecting here, upon returning…

皇上勵精圖治，思得天下才以理天下事，於是用科舉取士，一遵成憲，而加慎焉。《詩》所謂「古之人無斁，譽髦斯士」，此之謂也。廼成化十三年秋，應天府復當鄉試。府尹臣崇志豫以考試官請，上命臣健、臣經偕往。臣等受命祗懼，不敢宿留，亟乘傳而南。比至，重相戒飭，務秉至公，以奉德意。越三試，得其文之明於理
translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Yingtian Prefectural Provincial Examination

His Majesty vigourously strives for good governance and seeks to obtain the talents of the realm in order to manage the affairs of the realm. Therefore, in employing the civil service examinations to select scholars, he wholly follows the established statutes while exercising even greater caution therein. When the Book of Odes (Shi) says, "The men of old were untiring; / They brought renown to these fine scholars," this is what is meant. Now, in the autumn of the thirteenth year of the Chenghua era (1477), Yingtian Prefecture was once again scheduled to hold the Provincial Examination. The Prefectural Governor, Your Servant Chongzhi, petitioned in advance for Examiners, and His Majesty commanded Your Servant Jian and Your Servant Jing to go together. Receiving the command with reverent trepidation, Your Servants did not dare to tarry, but hastily rode the post south. Upon arriving, we solemnly admonished one another, resolving to uphold the utmost impartiality so as to carry out His Majesty's virtuous intentions. After the three examination sessions, we obtained those whose essays were clear in principle…

title: 成化十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
而足以適諸用者如
制額故事有錄臣經當序諸後
竊惟
天之生才固將以為世用也然不
有以養之則奚以成不有以
試之則奚以知有國者亦奚
從而用之是故三物有教三
===
年大比自成周為然矣我
國家稽古建學徧天下柬擇俊
秀以充生員飾其冠衣豐其
廩餼導以師儒董以憲臣非
易書詩禮春秋之經不讀非
孔曾思孟濂洛關閩之學不
講此養才之法也教養既久

punctuated: 而足以適諸用者，如制額。故事有錄，臣經當序諸後。竊惟天之生才，固將以為世用也。然不有以養之，則奚以成？不有以試之，則奚以知？有國者亦奚從而用之？是故三物有教，三年大比，自成周為然矣。我國家稽古建學，徧天下柬擇俊秀以充生員，飾其冠衣，豐其廩餼，導以師儒，董以憲臣；非《易》、《書》、《詩》、《禮》、《春秋》之經不讀，非孔、曾、思、孟、濂、洛、關、閩之學不講：此養才之法也。教養既久，
translation_en:
…and sufficient to be suited for practical application, matching the imperially decreed quota. By precedent there is an examination record, and your servant Jing ought to write the postface at the end.

I humbly reflect that when Heaven brings forth talent, it is surely intended for the use of the world. Yet if there is no means to nurture them, how can they be brought to completion? If there is no means to test them, how can they be known? And how then would those who possess the state be able to employ them? For this reason, instruction in the Three Things (sanwu) and the triennial Great Comparison (dabi) have been practiced since the era of Accomplished Zhou.

Our dynasty, examining antiquity, has established schools throughout the empire, selecting men of outstanding promise to serve as Government Students (shengyuan). It adorns their caps and robes, makes generous their stipends of grain, guides them through Confucian teachers, and supervises them through Censorate officials. No classics other than the Changes (Yi), Documents (Shu), Odes (Shi), Rites (Li), and Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) are read; no learning other than that of Confucius, Zengzi, Zisi, Mencius, and the masters of Lian, Luo, Guan, and Min is expounded: this is the method of nurturing talent. Once instruction and nurturing have been carried on for a long time,…

title: 成化十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
才無弗成於是自一邑一郡
以達于藩省自藩省以達于
禮部自禮部以進于
大廷初試以義再試以論詔誥
表判三試以策終奉
天子之詢治道賜出身此選才之
法也夫養之於未選之前者
===
如此其至選之於既養之後
者如此其嚴然後論辨而官
之或德進或事舉如鄧林之
材雖小大長短不一而取之
以為棟為梁為榱為桷無弗
可者矣然則我

法也夫養之於未選之前者
===
如此其至選之於既養之後
者如此其嚴然後論辨而官
之或德進或事舉如鄧林之
材雖小大長短不一而取之
以為東為梁為榱為桷無弗
可者矣然則我
祖宗
punctuated: 才無弗成。於是自一邑一郡以達于藩省，自藩省以達于禮部，自禮部以進于大廷。初試以義，再試以論、詔、誥、表、判，三試以策，終奉天子之詢治道，賜出身。此選才之法也。夫養之於未選之前者如此其至，選之於既養之後者如此其嚴，然後論辨而官之，或德進，或事舉，如鄧林之材，雖小大長短不一，而取之以為棟、為梁、為榱、為桷，無弗可者矣。然則我祖宗
translation_en: …there are no talents that do not reach completion. Thereupon, they advance from each district and prefecture to the province, from the province to the Ministry of Rites, and from the Ministry of Rites to the great Imperial Court. In the first session, they are examined with expositions on the Classics and Four Books; in the second session, with discourses, imperial edicts, mandates, memorials, and legal judgments; and in the third session, with policy questions; finally, they respectfully receive the Son of Heaven's inquiry into the way of governance and are granted civil service qualification. This is the method for selecting talent. Now, nurturing them before they are selected is thus so thorough, and selecting them after they have been nurtured is thus so rigorous; only after this are their merits evaluated and offices assigned to them. Some are promoted for their virtue, others are recommended for their administrative achievements—just like the timber of the Forest of Deng, which, though varying in size and length, can be taken to serve as ridgepoles, beams, rafters, or square rafters, with none proving unsuitable. This being so, that whereby our Imperial Ancestors…

title: 成化十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
列聖所以奉
天而治天下也豈不追儷隆古也
哉故百餘年来得才以亮天
工熈庶績者極濟濟藹藹雖
棫樸卷阿之盛奚以過焉京
畿首善之地士生其間沐

===

translation_en: …and the succession of Sacred Emperors have served Heaven and governed the realm—does it not rival high antiquity! Thus, for over a hundred years, the men of talent obtained to assist in Heaven's work and make all achievements shine forth have been most numerous and harmonious; even the flourishing eras celebrated in the odes "Yupu" (Thickly Growing Oaks) and "Quan'e" (Curving Slope) could not surpass this. title: 成化十三年應天府鄉試錄
text:
吾猶人也躬行君子則吾未
之有得夫孔子大聖也而猶
云然則諸士子烏可恃此而
畫乎其尚以聖賢之學自勵
必益厪於格物致知誠意正
心以脩其身以齊其家以需
聖天子他日之用由是推□□
===
平天下豈不誠豪傑之□□
若然則於
天與我之才
聖朝養我之恩斯不負矣而今日
與選才者不亦有光乎是用
書以為勸

翰林院侍讀周經謹序。
translation_en:
…I am perhaps equal to other men; as for personally carrying out the way of the gentleman, that I have not yet achieved." Now Confucius was a great sage, and yet he spoke thus; how then can the scholars rely on this and stop short? May they spur themselves on with the learning of the sages and worthies, devoting ever more diligence to investigating things, extending knowledge, making the intentions sincere, and rectifying the mind, so as to cultivate their persons and regulate their families, in readiness for the Sacred Son of Heaven's future use. Extending this to [governing the state and] bringing peace to All-under-Heaven, will they not truly be heroic [scholars]? If so, then they will not fail the talent that Heaven has bestowed upon us, nor the grace by which the Sacred Dynasty has nurtured us; and will those who took part in selecting talent today not also share in the glory? For this reason I write this as an exhortation.
Respectfully prefaced by Zhou Jing 周經, Expositor-in-waiting of the Hanlin Academy.
